Theoretical analysis In this section, we analyze the theoretical properties of Contextual Priority Attention, particularly its relationship to standard self-attention and its capacity to model dependencies in sequential data. Relationship to standard self-attention Standard self-attention computes attention weights as: 12 where are the query and key vectors for tokens i and j, respectively. We can show that under certain conditions, CPA approximates this pairwise attention mechanism. Specifically, if our priority scoring function is structured as: 13 where is a weighted sum of all key vectors (our Global Context Vector), then CPA implicitly captures pairwise interactions through this shared context. Proposition 1 Let be the attention matrix from standard self-attention, and let be the attention weights from CPA. If the GCV is computed as with weights proportional to the importance of token j in the sequence, then there exists a parameterization of the priority scoring function such that 14 The proof is provided in Appendix . The key insight is that CPA's prioritization based on global context provides an efficient proxy for explicit token-to-token attention when the context sufficiently represents the relevant aspects of all tokens. Expressive power A natural question is whether CPA can express the same functions as standard self-attention. We prove that: Theorem 1 For any self-attention mechanism with weights , there exists a parameterization of CPA that can approximate the function computed by this self-attention mechanism to arbitrary precision, provided the dimension of the Global Context Vector is sufficiently large. The proof, outlined in Appendix, relies on the universal approximation capabilities of neural networks30 and the fact that our priority scoring MLP can learn to extract token-specific queries from the global context. With sufficient capacity, the priority scoring function can learn to attend to the same tokens that would receive high attention weights in the standard mechanism. Practical implementation: While Theorem 1 is an existence proof establishing that CPA can theoretically approximate standard attention with a sufficiently large GCV, in our experiments we use a GCV of dimension (i.e., the same as the model dimension). This choice: Does not grow with sequence length n, maintaining constant parameter count Matches the dimensionality of keys and queries in standard Transformers Empirically provides sufficient representational capacity for all tested tasks (section "Results and analysis") The theorem's "sufficient capacity" condition is satisfied by the MLP's hidden dimension ( in our experiments) rather than by increasing the GCV dimension. We found no benefit from using even for sequences up to 32K tokens. While this theoretical result establishes that CPA has the expressive capacity to approximate standard attention, in practice, the inductive biases of the two approaches differ significantly, leading to different learning dynamics and generalization properties. Complexity-expressivity tradeoff We analyze the tradeoff between computational complexity and model expressivity for different attention variants: Standard self-attention: complexity, full expressivity. Linear attention (e.g., Performers): complexity, reduced expressivity due to kernel approximation. Pattern-based sparse attention: complexity where , limited by fixed patterns. CPA (our approach): theoretical complexity with experimentally observed linear scaling, expressivity modulated by GCV capacity. Figure 4 visualizes this tradeoff for various attention mechanisms. Unlike kernel-based methods, CPA doesn't rely on specific mathematical properties of the attention function. Instead, it learns to extract and use relevant global context, potentially capturing higher-order interactions that aren't easily expressible with fixed kernels. Fig. 4. Open in a new tab Theoretical trade-off between computational complexity and expressivity for different attention mechanisms. The arrow indicates the ideal direction (lower complexity, higher expressivity). CPA achieves a favorable balance by maintaining linear complexity while preserving much of the expressivity of standard attention. Information bottleneck perspective The Global Context Vector in CPA can be viewed through the lens of the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle25. The GCV creates a compressed representation of the input sequence, retaining the most relevant information while discarding noise. Proposition 2 Under the Information Bottleneck framework, the optimal Global Context Vector is one that maximizes , where denotes mutual information, is the input sequence, Y is the target output, and controls the compression-relevance tradeoff. This perspective provides theoretical justification for why CPA works well: it implicitly performs a form of information bottleneck, focusing on the most task-relevant aspects of the input sequence while filtering out irrelevant details. Experimental setup We evaluate CPA on a diverse set of tasks to assess its performance across different domains and sequence lengths. Our evaluation focuses on comparing CPA against standard self-attention and state-of-the-art efficient attention mechanisms. Model configurations CPA application in different architectures For encoder-decoder tasks (machine translation, summarization), we apply CPA to replace self-attention in the encoder only. The decoder employs standard masked self-attention for auto-regressive generation and standard cross-attention to attend to encoder outputs. This design choice offers several advantages: The encoder's Global Context Vector is computed once for the entire source sequence and remains fixed during decoding, ensuring efficient inference. The decoder's standard attention preserves the ability to attend to all previously generated tokens without modification. Cross-attention maintains full expressivity for encoder-decoder alignment. For encoder-only tasks (classification, language modeling with fixed context), CPA replaces all self-attention layers. For all model variants, we keep other components (feed-forward networks, layer normalization, residual connections) unchanged. Developing an efficient causal variant of CPA for decoder-only auto-regressive models is a promising direction for future work, which we discuss in section "Future directions". For fair comparison, we maintain the same model size (number of parameters) across all compared models by appropriately adjusting the hidden dimensions. We consider four variants of our approach: CPA-Avg: Using learned weighted averaging for GCV CPA-CLS: Using a [CLS] token approach for GCV CPA-CNN: Using a convolutional network with global pooling for GCV CPA-BERT: A BERT-style model with CPA replacing self-attention For all CPA variants, we use the two-layer MLP priority scoring function with hidden dimension , and the sparsemax transformation for sparse attention allocation unless otherwise specified. Baselines We compare against the following baselines: Standard Transformer1: The original Transformer with full self-attention Sparse Transformer2: Uses fixed sparse attention patterns Longformer8: Combines local windowed attention with global tokens Linformer4: Uses low-rank approximation of attention Performer5: Uses kernel-based approximation Reformer3: Uses locality-sensitive hashing BigBird10: Combines random, global, and local attention patterns We use the official implementations of these baselines with their recommended configurations, adjusting model sizes to match parameter counts for fair comparison. Tasks and datasets We evaluate on the following tasks and datasets: Machine translation: WMT14 English-German (En-De): 4.5M sentence pairs, evaluated with BLEU score WMT14 English-French (En-Fr): 36M sentence pairs, evaluated with BLEU score Language modeling: WikiText-10331: 103M tokens from Wikipedia articles, evaluated with perplexity PG1932: 28K books from Project Gutenberg, evaluated with perplexity Long document classification: Long Range Arena (LRA) benchmark33: A suite of tasks designed to test the ability to handle long-range dependencies IMDB Movie Reviews34: 50K movie reviews for sentiment analysis Hyperpartisan News Detection35: Articles labeled as hyperpartisan or not Question answering: SQuAD v1.1 and v2.036,37: Stanford Question Answering Dataset Natural Questions (NQ)38: Questions from real Google search queries TriviaQA39: Question-answer pairs from trivia competitions Long-context generation: CNN/Daily Mail summarization40: News articles with abstractive summaries arXiv paper summarization41: Scientific papers with abstracts as summaries Implementation details Our implementation is based on PyTorch42 and the HuggingFace Transformers library43. The sparse transformations (sparsemax and top-k Gumbel-Softmax) are implemented using custom CUDA kernels for efficiency. We employ mixed-precision training using NVIDIA Apex for all experiments. For machine translation tasks, we follow the standard Transformer base configuration1 with 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers, 8 attention heads, and 512-dimensional embeddings. For other tasks, we adjust model size according to task complexity and dataset size, ensuring fair comparison across all models. Detailed model configurations for each task are provided in Appendix. Training details We train all models using the Adam optimizer44 with a transformer-standard learning rate schedule: 15 We use label smoothing of 0.1 for classification tasks and dropout with probability 0.1 for all layers. Models are trained on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs with mixed precision training. For each task, we select hyperparameters based on validation performance. We employ early stopping based on validation performance with a patience of 10 epochs. To ensure reproducibility, we use five different random seeds for each experiment and report the mean and standard deviation of the results. Evaluation metrics We use task-specific evaluation metrics: BLEU scores for machine translation, computed using SacreBLEU451 to ensure reproducibility and fair comparison with prior work Perplexity for language modeling Accuracy for classification tasks F1 and Exact Match scores for question answering ROUGE scores (R-1, R-2, R-L) for summarization Additionally, we measure: Training time (hours) Peak memory usage (GB) Inference speed (tokens/second) FLOPs per sequence Model parameter count All runtime and memory measurements are conducted on identical hardware configurations to ensure fair comparison. Results and analysis Performance across tasks Table 2 presents the main results across all tasks, comparing CPA variants with baseline models. For brevity, we report results for the best-performing CPA variant (CPA-Avg) in the main table and provide detailed comparisons between all CPA variants in Appendix. Table 2. Results are averaged over 5 runs with different random seeds; standard deviations are shown in parentheses. Our findings indicate that CPA achieves competitive performance with standard Transformers across all tasks, with performance differences generally within 0.5 points. Among efficient attention variants, CPA-Avg consistently achieves strong results, ranking as first or second-best among efficient attention methods on all benchmarks. On tasks involving long sequences (LRA benchmark and document summarization), CPA demonstrates particularly strong results, outperforming most efficient attention alternatives by a significant margin. This suggests that our global-context approach effectively captures long-range dependencies without requiring quadratic computation. Figure 5 shows detailed performance on the Long Range Arena benchmark, which specifically tests models' ability to handle long sequences. CPA excels on tasks requiring long-range modeling, such as the Text and Retrieval subtasks, while maintaining competitive performance on other subtasks. Fig. 5. Learn more: PMC Disclaimer | PMC Copyright Notice Sci Rep. 2025 Dec 17;16:2869. doi: 10.1038/s41598-025-32639-x Contextual priority attention enables linear time sequence modeling in transformers Karim Ben Khaled 1,2,?, Davy Monticolo 1,2 Author information Article notes Copyright and License information PMCID: PMC12828051 PMID: 41408385 Abstract The quadratic computational complexity of the self-attention mechanism in Transformer models severely constrains their applicability to long sequence inputs. We propose Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), a novel attention mechanism that reduces computational complexity from to theoretically, with experimentally observed linear scaling, while preserving the essential contextual modeling capabilities of traditional attention. Unlike existing efficient attention variants that approximate the full attention matrix, CPA fundamentally reimagines attention as a global-context-driven priority system. Our approach first computes a Global Context Vector (GCV) to capture the overall sequence information, then uses this context to assign priority scores to individual tokens, enabling sparse attention allocation. In encoder-decoder architectures, we apply CPA to the encoder while maintaining standard attention in the decoder, achieving substantial efficiency improvements while preserving full model expressivity for sequence-to-sequence tasks. Through theoretical analysis and extensive experimentation across language understanding, translation, and long document tasks, we demonstrate that CPA achieves comparable performance to standard self-attention while offering significant efficiency gains. On long-sequence benchmarks (8K+ tokens), CPA outperforms traditional Transformers and state-of-the-art efficient attention variants while using substantially fewer computational resources. Our findings suggest that pairwise token interactions may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling, opening new avenues for efficient large-scale language models. Subject terms: Engineering, Mathematics and computing Introduction Transformer-based models1 have revolutionized natural language processing and many other domains of artificial intelligence. Their success stems largely from the self-attention mechanism, which enables each element in a sequence to attend to all other elements, capturing complex dependencies regardless of positional distance. However, this attention mechanism scales quadratically with sequence length, leading to significant computational and memory constraints when processing long inputs. This quadratic scaling poses a fundamental challenge for applications requiring long context, such as document-level machine translation, long-form question answering, and whole-document analysis. While various approaches have been proposed to address this bottleneck2-5, most attempt to approximate standard self-attention through techniques such as low-rank approximations, localized attention patterns, or kernel methods. In this paper, we introduce Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), which takes a fundamentally different approach. Rather than approximating the pairwise attention matrix, CPA reimagines attention as a global-to-local relevance filtering process inspired by cognitive theories of human attention6,7. Our approach first computes a Global Context Vector (GCV) that captures the "big picture" of the input sequence. Then, using this global context, we compute a priority score for each input element, measuring its relevance to the current context. Finally, we apply a sparse transformation to these scores, allowing the model to focus exclusively on the most relevant elements (see Fig. 1). Fig. 1. Open in a new tab Overview of the Contextual Priority Attention mechanism. (a) First, a Global Context Vector (GCV) is computed from the input sequence using a learned weighted average. (b) The GCV is concatenated with each token to compute token-specific priority scores via an MLP. (c) Sparse attention weights are generated by applying sparsemax to the priority scores. (d) The output is computed as a weighted sum of value projections, using only tokens with non-zero attention weights. CPA offers several key advantages: Linear computational complexity () with respect to sequence length Interpretable attention patterns with explicit token prioritization Adaptive sparsity that adjusts to input complexity Theoretical capacity to capture both local and global dependencies Through extensive experimentation on multiple tasks including machine translation, language modeling, and long document classification, we demonstrate that CPA achieves performance competitive with full attention while significantly reducing computational requirements, especially for long sequences. Our contributions are as follows: We propose Contextual Priority Attention, a novel attention mechanism with theoretical complexity that empirically demonstrates linear scaling, based on global-context-driven prioritization. We provide theoretical analysis showing that CPA can approximate full attention under certain conditions while maintaining linear complexity. We empirically demonstrate competitive performance with state-of-the-art models across multiple tasks. We analyze the emergent attention patterns, showing how CPA learns meaningful prioritization strategies. Related work Efficient attention mechanisms The quadratic complexity of self-attention has inspired numerous approaches to improve efficiency. These can be broadly categorized into several strategies: Pattern-based sparsity: Methods like Sparse Transformer2 and Longformer8 limit attention to predefined patterns, such as local windows, dilated windows, or fixed global tokens. BlockBERT9 and BigBird10 use block-sparse attention patterns. While effective, these approaches incorporate structural biases that may not align with the actual dependencies in the data. Learnable sparsity: Methods such as Reformer3 use locality-sensitive hashing to dynamically identify similar tokens that should attend to each other. Routing Transformer11 employs content-based clustering. These approaches reduce complexity but still fundamentally rely on pairwise token interactions. Low-rank approximations: Linformer4 projects the key and value matrices to lower dimensions, achieving linear complexity. However, this approach struggles with variable-length inputs and loses the flexibility of the original attention mechanism. Kernel methods: Performers5 and Linear Transformers12 rewrite the softmax attention using kernel methods, approximating the attention matrix implicitly. While mathematically elegant, these methods may sacrifice some of the expressivity of the original attention mechanism. Recurrence-based methods: Models like Transformer-XL13 and Compressive Transformer14 incorporate recurrence to handle long sequences. These approaches maintain the standard attention within segments but use recurrent connections between segments. Table 1 provides a comparative analysis of these approaches. Our Contextual Priority Attention differs fundamentally from these approaches by eliminating pairwise comparisons entirely, instead using global context to guide token-specific attention allocation. Table 1. Comparison of efficient attention approaches. Approach Complexity Preserves full expressivity Handles variable length inputs Learnable patterns Implementation complexity Standard attention Low Pattern-based Sparsity Medium Learnable Sparsity Partial High Low-Rank Approximations Partial Medium Kernel Methods Partial Partial Medium Recurrence-based + Memory Partial High CPA (Ours) Theoretical Medium Open in a new tab Cognitive models of attention Our approach is loosely inspired by cognitive theories of human attention, which suggest that perception involves both bottom-up feature processing and top-down attentional control guided by current goals and context15,16. Particularly relevant is Broadbent's filter theory7, which proposes that cognitive processing employs selective filters to focus only on relevant stimuli. In neuroscience, the interaction between global brain states and local neural activity parallels our approach of using global context to guide local attention allocation17. Several computational models of attention in computer vision have implemented related concepts, particularly through top-down modulation of bottom-up saliency18,19. Sparse neural networks Our work also relates to research on sparse neural networks, particularly approaches that dynamically determine sparsity patterns. Techniques such as Sparse Mixture of Experts20,21 and conditional computation22,23 activate only relevant parts of the network based on input. These approaches demonstrate that sparse activation can achieve strong performance while improving computational efficiency. Contextual priority attention In this section, we describe our proposed Contextual Priority Attention mechanism in detail, first presenting the intuition and then formalizing the approach. Intuition Traditional self-attention computes pairwise interactions between all tokens in a sequence, requiring comparisons for a sequence of length n. This exhaustive approach implicitly assumes that every token-to-token relationship is potentially informative and must be explicitly evaluated. However, this assumption may be unnecessarily conservative for many natural language tasks, where the semantic content of a sequence can often be summarized more compactly. Human attention operates fundamentally differently. Cognitive research suggests that we do not exhaustively compare every perceived element to every other element. Instead, we rapidly construct a holistic understanding of our environment-a "gist" or mental model-and then selectively attend to elements that are most relevant to our current goals and context16,24. This two-stage process of global comprehension followed by selective focus allows humans to efficiently process complex scenes without cognitive overload. CPA draws direct inspiration from this cognitive model. Rather than asking "how relevant is token A to token B?" for all possible pairs, we decompose attention into two sequential stages: Global comprehension: First, we compute a Global Context Vector (GCV) that captures a compressed, holistic representation of the entire input sequence. This vector serves as a summary of "what is this sequence about?" Selective prioritization: Then, for each token, we evaluate a single question: "how relevant is this token to the global context?" This yields a priority score indicating contextual importance. This reformulation reduces the computational burden from pairwise comparisons to n context-relative evaluations, while preserving the essential selective nature of attention. Figure 2 illustrates this fundamental conceptual difference between standard self-attention and CPA. Fig. 2. Open in a new tab Conceptual comparison between standard self-attention (left) and Contextual Priority Attention (right). Standard attention computes all pairwise interactions between tokens, resulting in quadratic complexity. CPA first computes a global context representation, then evaluates each token against this shared context, achieving linear complexity. To illustrate with a concrete example, consider processing the sentence: "The cat, which had been sleeping peacefully on the warm windowsill all afternoon, suddenly jumped down." Standard self-attention would compute interactions, including many between tokens with minimal semantic relationship (e.g., "peacefully" and "down"). In contrast, CPA first forms a global understanding that this sentence describes a cat's action, then prioritizes tokens most relevant to this context-likely "cat," "sleeping," and "jumped"-while assigning lower priority to modifiers and function words. This approach offers an additional benefit beyond computational efficiency: it provides an implicit regularization effect. By forcing the model to route all attention decisions through a shared global context, CPA encourages the learning of representations that capture semantically meaningful aspects of the input rather than spurious local correlations. The global context acts as an information bottleneck25, filtering out noise while retaining task-relevant signal. By computing relevance scores against a shared global context, we can prioritize tokens holistically, focusing computational resources on the most contextually important elements while naturally filtering out irrelevant ones. This design philosophy "global understanding before local selection" mirrors not only human cognition but also efficient algorithms in other domains, such as hierarchical search and coarse-to-fine processing in computer vision26. Contextual Priority Attention consists of four main components: Global Context Vector (GCV) The Global Context Vector captures a holistic representation of the input sequence. We explore multiple implementation strategies: Learned average: 1 where are learned weights computed as: 2 with being a learnable parameter vector. Neural summarization: We apply a small neural network to compress the sequence: 3 where could be implemented as a single-layer transformer encoder or a convolutional network with global pooling. In our experiments, the learned average approach offered the best balance of performance and efficiency. Priority scoring For each token , we compute a priority score indicating its contextual relevance: 4 where represents the concatenation of the token embedding and the global context vector, and MLP is a two-layer perceptron: 5 with , , , , h being the hidden dimension, and denoting the ReLU activation function. The priority scoring function effectively measures how relevant each token is to the current global context, without requiring pairwise comparisons between tokens. Sparse attention allocation To achieve sparse attention allocation, we transform the raw priority scores using a sparsemax28 or top-k Gumbel-Softmax29 function: 6 or 7 where is the vector of priority scores and represents the attention weight assigned to token i. Unlike softmax, which assigns non-zero weights to all tokens, these transformations produce truly sparse distributions, with many tokens receiving exactly zero attention. The parameter k in the top-k variant can be either fixed or dynamically computed based on input complexity. Training times are normalized relative to the standard Transformer at sequence length 512. The OOM results for standard Transformer occur during training when maintaining consistent batch sizes across all sequence lengths for fair comparison. With standard data parallelism, each GPU maintains a complete copy of the model, optimizer states, and gradients; thus, the 840GB = 320GB total memory cannot be pooled, and each GPU independently faces the 40GB memory constraint. The quadratic memory footprint includes: (1) the attention matrices (approximately 32GB per layer for batch size of 16 at 8192 tokens with mixed precision), (2) activation storage for backpropagation, (3) optimizer states (Adam requires 2 parameter memory), and (4) gradient accumulation. While it is possible to train longer sequences with reduced batch size or gradient checkpointing, we maintain consistent training configurations across all models for fair efficiency comparison. CPA demonstrates excellent scalability, with memory usage and computation time scaling linearly with sequence length. For short sequences (512 tokens), the efficiency gains are moderate compared to standard Transformers. However, as sequence length increases, the benefits become increasingly pronounced. At 8,192 tokens, standard Transformers run out of memory (OOM) on our hardware, while CPA continues to function efficiently. At 32,768 tokens, CPA maintains the lowest memory usage and highest inference speed among all compared models who went Out-Of-Memory. Figure 6 visualizes the scaling of memory usage with respect to sequence length, clearly showing the quadratic scaling of standard Transformers versus the linear scaling of CPA and other efficient attention variants. Subsequent rows show performance when removing or replacing each component. These results highlight the importance of each component: Using sparsemax instead of softmax provides a small but consistent performance improvement (+0.2 BLEU) The two-layer MLP for priority scoring is crucial for performance (+0.7 BLEU compared to linear) Multi-head attention remains important, as in standard Transformers (+1.3 BLEU versus single-head) The learned GCV provides meaningful gains over simple averaging (+0.5 BLEU) We also investigate how varying the sparsity level in our sparse attention allocation affects performance. Performance improves rapidly as sparsity decreases from 1% to approximately 25%, then plateaus. This suggests that attending to a small subset of tokens is sufficient to capture most necessary information. Performance improves rapidly as k increases from 1% to approximately 25% of the sequence length, then plateaus, suggesting that attending to a small subset of tokens is sufficient to capture most of the necessary information. Analysis of learned attention patterns To better understand how CPA allocates attention, we visualize the sparse attention weights for different layers and heads on the WMT14 En-De translation task. Figure 8 shows attention visualizations for representative heads in different layers. Fig. 8. Open in a new tab Visualization of learned attention patterns in CPA. Each colored bar represents a token receiving non-zero attention, with color intensity indicating attention weight magnitude. (a-c) show patterns from different layers and heads, demonstrating increasing specialization from early to deeper layers. (d) shows average attention by position across all heads in the final layer. We observe several interesting patterns: Specialization by head: Different attention heads focus on different aspects of the input. Some heads attend primarily to content words (nouns, verbs), while others focus on function words or syntactic markers. Layer-specific behavior: Early layers (Figure 8a) tend to have more distributed attention, while deeper layers (Figure 8c) become increasingly focused on specific tokens that are semantically important for the current context. Context-dependent sparsity: The number of tokens receiving non-zero attention varies significantly based on the input complexity. Simple sentences result in very sparse attention (5-10% of tokens), while complex sentences with ambiguous references or specialized terminology lead to less sparse patterns (20-30% of tokens). Positional biases: Despite not explicitly encoding positional relationships in the attention mechanism, certain heads develop positional biases (Figure 8d), focusing on tokens near the beginning or end of the sequence. These observations suggest that CPA learns meaningful attention allocation strategies that adapt to input complexity, supporting our hypothesis that explicit pairwise comparisons are often redundant. Discussion Key findings Our experimental results demonstrate that Contextual Priority Attention achieves performance competitive with standard self-attention while significantly reducing computational costs. This supports our hypothesis that explicit pairwise token interactions may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. The global-to-local attention paradigm of CPA offers several advantages: Efficiency: Linear scaling with sequence length enables processing of much longer sequences than standard Transformers can handle. Our results show CPA can efficiently process sequences up to 32K tokens, where standard Transformers run out of memory. Interpretability: The sparse attention patterns highlight which tokens are most contextually relevant, providing insights into model decision-making. As shown in our analysis of attention patterns, CPA learns meaningful token prioritization strategies. Adaptivity: The number of tokens attended to naturally adapts to input complexity, allocating computational resources where needed. This results in more efficient processing of simple inputs while maintaining capacity for complex ones. Effectiveness on long sequences: CPA performs particularly well on long document tasks, where capturing both local and global context is essential. This makes it well-suited for applications like document-level machine translation, long-form question answering, and document summarization. Figure 9 illustrates the performance-complexity trade-off for different attention mechanisms. CPA achieves an attractive balance, delivering near-standard-Transformer performance with linear computational complexity. Fig. 9. Open in a new tab Performance vs. computational complexity for different attention mechanisms on the WMT14 En-De translation task. The ideal models would be in the top-left corner (high performance, low complexity). CPA achieves a favorable trade-off, approaching the performance of standard Transformers while maintaining linear complexity. Limitations Despite its promising results, CPA has several limitations that present opportunities for future research: Global context quality: The performance of CPA depends critically on the quality of the Global Context Vector. For very complex or ambiguous inputs, a single context vector may not capture all relevant aspects of the sequence. This limitation becomes more pronounced as sequence length increases beyond the sizes tested in our experiments. Task-specific performance: While CPA performs well across most tasks, it shows slightly lower performance on certain language modeling benchmarks. This suggests that some tasks may benefit more from exhaustive pairwise comparisons. Training dynamics: We observed that CPA models sometimes require more careful initialization and training compared to standard Transformers, likely due to the increased importance of the global context representation. Learning meaningful global representations early in training is crucial for model convergence. Theoretical capacity: While we prove that CPA can theoretically approximate standard attention, this approximation may require higher model capacity in practice. Our experiments compensated for this by slightly increasing the hidden dimensions in the priority scoring MLP. Hardware utilization: The sparse attention patterns in CPA, while theoretically efficient, may not fully utilize modern GPU hardware designed for dense matrix operations. Custom CUDA kernels for sparse operations help mitigate this issue but introduce additional implementation complexity. Future directions Our work opens several promising directions for future research: Hierarchical CPA: Creating hierarchical representations of global context at different granularities could help capture both fine-grained and high-level patterns. This approach would involve computing multiple context vectors at different levels of abstraction, from local windows to global document-level representations. Adaptive sparsity: Dynamically adjusting the sparsity level based on input complexity could further improve efficiency without sacrificing performance. This could be implemented by learning a threshold function that determines the minimum attention weight required for a token to be considered relevant. Causal CPA for auto-regressive generation: Our current implementation applies CPA only in encoder architectures. Extending CPA to efficient causal decoding in decoder-only models (like GPT-style architectures) requires careful design to handle incremental GCV updates. One promising approach is to maintain a running GCV that can be updated in time per generated token: . This would enable linear-time auto-regressive generation while maintaining the benefits of global context-driven attention. Cross-modal applications: The global context approach may be particularly well-suited for cross-modal attention, where different modalities (text, image, audio) require different attention patterns. For example, in multimodal tasks, separate global context vectors could be computed for each modality, then used to guide cross-modal attention. Theoretical exploration: Further theoretical analysis of the expressivity-efficiency tradeoff in different attention mechanisms could guide the development of even more efficient variants. This includes a deeper understanding of what types of dependencies can be captured by global-context-based attention versus explicit pairwise attention. Pre-training and transfer learning: Investigating how CPA performs in large-scale pre-training scenarios and subsequent fine-tuning could reveal its potential for more efficient foundation models. The linear scaling properties of CPA make it particularly promising for very large models trained on extensive datasets. Hardware optimization: CPA's sparse attention patterns could enable specialized hardware implementations for even greater efficiency gains. Future research could explore hardware designs specifically optimized for global-context-based sparse attention mechanisms. Figure 10 illustrates these potential future directions, highlighting their relative complexity and potential impact. We believe the hierarchical CPA and adaptive sparsity approaches represent the most immediate opportunities for significant improvements. Fig. 10. Open in a new tab Potential future directions for extending Contextual Priority Attention. Each path represents a promising avenue for research, with estimated complexity and potential impact. Conclusion We presented Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), a novel attention mechanism that achieves theoretical complexity while empirically demonstrating linear scaling and maintaining competitive performance with standard Transformers. By reimagining attention as a global-context-driven priority system rather than exhaustive pairwise comparisons, CPA offers significant efficiency improvements, particularly for long sequences. Our experimental results across diverse tasks demonstrate that CPA achieves performance comparable to full attention while scaling more efficiently to long inputs. The emergent attention patterns reveal that CPA learns meaningful prioritization strategies that adapt to input complexity. On the Long Range Arena benchmark specifically designed to test long-range modeling capabilities, CPA outperforms other efficient attention variants by a significant margin. The success of CPA suggests that the quadratic computational complexity of standard self-attention may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. By focusing computational resources on the most contextually relevant tokens, CPA provides an efficient alternative that scales better to the increasingly long contexts required by modern NLP applications. The ability to process sequences of tens of thousands of tokens efficiently opens up new possibilities for applications such as document-level translation, long-form question answering, and full-document summarization. Since the hidden dimension h and model dimension d are fixed hyperparameters for a given model architecture, this simplifies to theoretically. However, in practice, for all realistic sequence lengths and model dimensions (e.g., , , -13 for ), the ndh term dominates the term, resulting in effectively linear scaling with sequence length. This is confirmed empirically by our scaling experiments in Figs. 3 and 6, where CPA demonstrates linear growth comparable to other methods like Linformer and Performer. This represents a significant improvement over the complexity of standard self-attention. Fig. 3. CPA demonstrates linear scaling in practice (despite theoretical complexity), matching other efficient attention variants, while standard self-attention scales quadratically. See section "Computational complexity" for detailed complexity analysis. Fig. 6. Open in a new tab Peak memory usage as a function of sequence length. Standard Transformer shows quadratic scaling, while CPA and other efficient variants scale linearly. CPA consistently requires less memory than other efficient attention alternatives. Incorporating positional information To maintain the Transformer's ability to model sequence order, we incorporate positional information by adding positional encodings to the input embeddings before computing the GCV and priority scores: 11 where is the positional encoding for position i, implemented using either the sinusoidal encodings from Vaswani et al.1 or learned positional embeddings. Theoretical analysis In this section, we analyze the theoretical properties of Contextual Priority Attention, particularly its relationship to standard self-attention and its capacity to model dependencies in sequential data. Relationship to standard self-attention Standard self-attention computes attention weights as: 12 where are the query and key vectors for tokens i and j, respectively. We can show that under certain conditions, CPA approximates this pairwise attention mechanism. Specifically, if our priority scoring function is structured as: 13 where is a weighted sum of all key vectors (our Global Context Vector), then CPA implicitly captures pairwise interactions through this shared context. Proposition 1 Let be the attention matrix from standard self-attention, and let be the attention weights from CPA. If the GCV is computed as with weights proportional to the importance of token j in the sequence, then there exists a parameterization of the priority scoring function such that 14 The proof is provided in Appendix . The key insight is that CPA's prioritization based on global context provides an efficient proxy for explicit token-to-token attention when the context sufficiently represents the relevant aspects of all tokens. Expressive power A natural question is whether CPA can express the same functions as standard self-attention. We prove that: Theorem 1 For any self-attention mechanism with weights , there exists a parameterization of CPA that can approximate the function computed by this self-attention mechanism to arbitrary precision, provided the dimension of the Global Context Vector is sufficiently large. The proof, outlined in Appendix, relies on the universal approximation capabilities of neural networks30 and the fact that our priority scoring MLP can learn to extract token-specific queries from the global context. With sufficient capacity, the priority scoring function can learn to attend to the same tokens that would receive high attention weights in the standard mechanism. Practical implementation: While Theorem 1 is an existence proof establishing that CPA can theoretically approximate standard attention with a sufficiently large GCV, in our experiments we use a GCV of dimension (i.e., the same as the model dimension). This choice: Does not grow with sequence length n, maintaining constant parameter count Matches the dimensionality of keys and queries in standard Transformers Empirically provides sufficient representational capacity for all tested tasks (section "Results and analysis") The theorem's "sufficient capacity" condition is satisfied by the MLP's hidden dimension ( in our experiments) rather than by increasing the GCV dimension. We found no benefit from using even for sequences up to 32K tokens. While this theoretical result establishes that CPA has the expressive capacity to approximate standard attention, in practice, the inductive biases of the two approaches differ significantly, leading to different learning dynamics and generalization properties. Complexity-expressivity tradeoff We analyze the tradeoff between computational complexity and model expressivity for different attention variants: Standard self-attention: complexity, full expressivity. Linear attention (e.g., Performers): complexity, reduced expressivity due to kernel approximation. Pattern-based sparse attention: complexity where , limited by fixed patterns. CPA (our approach): theoretical complexity with experimentally observed linear scaling, expressivity modulated by GCV capacity. Figure 4 visualizes this tradeoff for various attention mechanisms. Unlike kernel-based methods, CPA doesn't rely on specific mathematical properties of the attention function. Instead, it learns to extract and use relevant global context, potentially capturing higher-order interactions that aren't easily expressible with fixed kernels. Fig. 4. Open in a new tab Theoretical trade-off between computational complexity and expressivity for different attention mechanisms. The arrow indicates the ideal direction (lower complexity, higher expressivity). CPA achieves a favorable balance by maintaining linear complexity while preserving much of the expressivity of standard attention. Information bottleneck perspective The Global Context Vector in CPA can be viewed through the lens of the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle25. The GCV creates a compressed representation of the input sequence, retaining the most relevant information while discarding noise. Proposition 2 Under the Information Bottleneck framework, the optimal Global Context Vector is one that maximizes , where denotes mutual information, is the input sequence, Y is the target output, and controls the compression-relevance tradeoff. This perspective provides theoretical justification for why CPA works well: it implicitly performs a form of information bottleneck, focusing on the most task-relevant aspects of the input sequence while filtering out irrelevant details. Experimental setup We evaluate CPA on a diverse set of tasks to assess its performance across different domains and sequence lengths. Our evaluation focuses on comparing CPA against standard self-attention and state-of-the-art efficient attention mechanisms. Model configurations CPA application in different architectures For encoder-decoder tasks (machine translation, summarization), we apply CPA to replace self-attention in the encoder only. The decoder employs standard masked self-attention for auto-regressive generation and standard cross-attention to attend to encoder outputs. This design choice offers several advantages: The encoder's Global Context Vector is computed once for the entire source sequence and remains fixed during decoding, ensuring efficient inference. The decoder's standard attention preserves the ability to attend to all previously generated tokens without modification. Cross-attention maintains full expressivity for encoder-decoder alignment. For encoder-only tasks (classification, language modeling with fixed context), CPA replaces all self-attention layers. For all model variants, we keep other components (feed-forward networks, layer normalization, residual connections) unchanged. Developing an efficient causal variant of CPA for decoder-only auto-regressive models is a promising direction for future work, which we discuss in section "Future directions". For fair comparison, we maintain the same model size (number of parameters) across all compared models by appropriately adjusting the hidden dimensions. We consider four variants of our approach: CPA-Avg: Using learned weighted averaging for GCV CPA-CLS: Using a [CLS] token approach for GCV CPA-CNN: Using a convolutional network with global pooling for GCV CPA-BERT: A BERT-style model with CPA replacing self-attention For all CPA variants, we use the two-layer MLP priority scoring function with hidden dimension , and the sparsemax transformation for sparse attention allocation unless otherwise specified. Baselines We compare against the following baselines: Standard Transformer1: The original Transformer with full self-attention Sparse Transformer2: Uses fixed sparse attention patterns Longformer8: Combines local windowed attention with global tokens Linformer4: Uses low-rank approximation of attention Performer5: Uses kernel-based approximation Reformer3: Uses locality-sensitive hashing BigBird10: Combines random, global, and local attention patterns We use the official implementations of these baselines with their recommended configurations, adjusting model sizes to match parameter counts for fair comparison. Tasks and datasets We evaluate on the following tasks and datasets: Machine translation: WMT14 English-German (En-De): 4.5M sentence pairs, evaluated with BLEU score WMT14 English-French (En-Fr): 36M sentence pairs, evaluated with BLEU score Language modeling: WikiText-10331: 103M tokens from Wikipedia articles, evaluated with perplexity PG1932: 28K books from Project Gutenberg, evaluated with perplexity Long document classification: Long Range Arena (LRA) benchmark33: A suite of tasks designed to test the ability to handle long-range dependencies IMDB Movie Reviews34: 50K movie reviews for sentiment analysis Hyperpartisan News Detection35: Articles labeled as hyperpartisan or not Question answering: SQuAD v1.1 and v2.036,37: Stanford Question Answering Dataset Natural Questions (NQ)38: Questions from real Google search queries TriviaQA39: Question-answer pairs from trivia competitions Long-context generation: CNN/Daily Mail summarization40: News articles with abstractive summaries arXiv paper summarization41: Scientific papers with abstracts as summaries Implementation details Our implementation is based on PyTorch42 and the HuggingFace Transformers library43. The sparse transformations (sparsemax and top-k Gumbel-Softmax) are implemented using custom CUDA kernels for efficiency. We employ mixed-precision training using NVIDIA Apex for all experiments. For machine translation tasks, we follow the standard Transformer base configuration1 with 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers, 8 attention heads, and 512-dimensional embeddings. For other tasks, we adjust model size according to task complexity and dataset size, ensuring fair comparison across all models. Detailed model configurations for each task are provided in Appendix. Training details We train all models using the Adam optimizer44 with a transformer-standard learning rate schedule: 15 We use label smoothing of 0.1 for classification tasks and dropout with probability 0.1 for all layers. Models are trained on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs with mixed precision training. For each task, we select hyperparameters based on validation performance. We employ early stopping based on validation performance with a patience of 10 epochs. To ensure reproducibility, we use five different random seeds for each experiment and report the mean and standard deviation of the results. Evaluation metrics We use task-specific evaluation metrics: BLEU scores for machine translation, computed using SacreBLEU451 to ensure reproducibility and fair comparison with prior work Perplexity for language modeling Accuracy for classification tasks F1 and Exact Match scores for question answering ROUGE scores (R-1, R-2, R-L) for summarization Additionally, we measure: Training time (hours) Peak memory usage (GB) Inference speed (tokens/second) FLOPs per sequence Model parameter count All runtime and memory measurements are conducted on identical hardware configurations to ensure fair comparison. For brevity, we report results for the best-performing CPA variant (CPA-Avg) in the main table and provide detailed comparisons between all CPA variants in Appendix. Table 2. Our findings indicate that CPA achieves competitive performance with standard Transformers across all tasks, with performance differences generally within 0.5 points. Among efficient attention variants, CPA-Avg consistently achieves strong results, ranking as first or second-best among efficient attention methods on all benchmarks. On tasks involving long sequences (LRA benchmark and document summarization), CPA demonstrates particularly strong results, outperforming most efficient attention alternatives by a significant margin. This suggests that our global-context approach effectively captures long-range dependencies without requiring quadratic computation. Each path represents a promising avenue for research, with estimated complexity and potential impact. Conclusion We presented Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), a novel attention mechanism that achieves theoretical complexity while empirically demonstrating linear scaling and maintaining competitive performance with standard Transformers. By reimagining attention as a global-context-driven priority system rather than exhaustive pairwise comparisons, CPA offers significant efficiency improvements, particularly for long sequences. Our experimental results across diverse tasks demonstrate that CPA achieves performance comparable to full attention while scaling more efficiently to long inputs. The emergent attention patterns reveal that CPA learns meaningful prioritization strategies that adapt to input complexity. On the Long Range Arena benchmark specifically designed to test long-range modeling capabilities, CPA outperforms other efficient attention variants by a significant margin. The success of CPA suggests that the quadratic computational complexity of standard self-attention may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. By focusing computational resources on the most contextually relevant tokens, CPA provides an efficient alternative that scales better to the increasingly long contexts required by modern NLP applications. Conclusion We presented Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), a novel attention mechanism that achieves theoretical complexity while empirically demonstrating linear scaling and maintaining competitive performance with standard Transformers. By reimagining attention as a global-context-driven priority system rather than exhaustive pairwise comparisons, CPA offers significant efficiency improvements, particularly for long sequences. Our experimental results across diverse tasks demonstrate that CPA achieves performance comparable to full attention while scaling more efficiently to long inputs. The emergent attention patterns reveal that CPA learns meaningful prioritization strategies that adapt to input complexity. On the Long Range Arena benchmark specifically designed to test long-range modeling capabilities, CPA outperforms other efficient attention variants by a significant margin. The success of CPA suggests that the quadratic computational complexity of standard self-attention may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. By focusing computational resources on the most contextually relevant tokens, CPA provides an efficient alternative that scales better to the increasingly long contexts required by modern NLP applications. The ability to process sequences of tens of thousands of tokens efficiently opens up new possibilities for applications such as document-level translation, long-form question answering, and full-document summarization. As models continue to scale and applications demand increasingly longer context windows, approaches like CPA that break the quadratic scaling barrier without significant performance degradation will become increasingly important. We believe this work represents an important step toward more efficient transformer architectures and hope that the global-context approach inspires further innovations in attention mechanisms. Future work will explore hierarchical extensions of CPA, dynamic sparsity approaches, and applications to multimodal tasks, further extending the capabilities of this promising approach. Tsinghua University Abstract Transformer-based architectures have become the prevailing backbone of large language models. However, the quadratic time and memory complexity of self-attention remains a fundamental obstacle to efficient long-context modeling. To address this limitation, recent research has introduced two principal categories of efficient attention mechanisms. Linear attention methods achieve linear complexity through kernel approximations, recurrent formulations, or fast- weight dynamics, thereby enabling scalable inference with reduced computational overhead. Sparse attention techniques, in contrast, limit attention computation to selected subsets of tokens based on fixed patterns, block-wise routing, or clustering strategies, enhancing efficiency while preserving contextual coverage. This survey provides a systematic and comprehensive overview of these developments, integrating both algorithmic innovations and hardware-level considerations. In addition, we analyze the incorporation of efficient attention into large- scale pre-trained language models, including both architectures built entirely on efficient attention and hybrid designs that combine local and global components. By aligning theoretical foundations with practical deployment strategies, this work aims to serve as a foundational reference for advancing the design of scalable and efficient language models. Introduction Transformer-based architectures [61] have become the de-facto choice as the backbone of modern Large Language Models (LLMs). Despite their success, the standard self-attention mechanism remains a significant computational bottleneck, with quadratic time and memory complexity with respect to input sequence length. This limitation poses substantial challenges for scaling LLMs to handle increasingly long contexts with both strong performance and high efficiency. To address this, two major directions have emerged to reduce the time and space complexity of softmax Attention. The first mechanism is Linear Attention [17, 22, 50, 53, 70, 72], which seeks to reduce attention complexity by reparameterizing or approximating the softmax attention as linear operations. The second candidate is Sparse Attention [ 8, 21, 34, 56, 73], which restricts attention computation to a subset of the full key space based on fixed or dynamic sparsity pat- terns. While both approaches aim to improve efficiency, they differ significantly in formulation, design choices, and hardware implications. This survey provides a comprehensive review of recent developments in Efficient Attention mechanisms, with a dual focus on algorithmic principles and system-level implementation. Based on that, we also study the Pre-trained LLM employing these Efficient Attentions. We categorize linear attention methods into three major paradigms. First, kernelized linear attention approximates the softmax kernel with inner products in a feature space, achieving linear complexity via random feature maps [ 9, 42] or fixed positive mappings [ 22]. Second, recurrent linear attention with forgetting mechanisms introduces position-aware recurrence, enabling long-sequence modeling through data-independent [53] or data-dependent decay [17, 70], which control how past information fades over time. Third, fast-weight and meta-learning- based formulations reinterpret linear attention as a memory update process optimized online, where models such as DeltaNet [50, 72] and TTT [51, 52] incorporate fast-learning dynamics directly into the state evolution. We also examine hardware-friendly representations of linear attention-including parallel, recurrent, and chunkwise forms-highlighting their respective trade-offs in computational complexity, memory footprint, and compatibility with training or inference workflows. We classify Sparse Attention into fixed-pattern sparsity, block sparsity, and clustering-based sparsity. Fixed-pattern sparsity adopts static token-level masks such as sliding windows, dilated positions, or designated global tokens, offering simplicity and hardware-friendliness [4, 8, 14, 65]. Block sparsity selects or routes attention at block granularity, either via heuristic scoring [34, 56, 66], trainable gating [15, 73], enabling structured memory access and efficient GPU utilization. Clustering-based sparsity organizes key-value pairs using content-based or position-aware grouping methods such as k-means or Local Sensitive Hashing (LSH), facilitating semantically aware retrieval with reduced memory overhead [7, 24, 32]. Finally, we also discuss bidirectional sparse designs extend sparsity patterns to encoder-style models. These approaches differ in sparsity granularity, selection mechanism, and their alignment with hardware primitives like FlashAttention [10], and collectively represent the foundation for efficient long-context modeling in modern Transformers. There are recent efforts to integrate efficient attention mechanisms into industry-level Pre- trained Language Models. These include both pure efficient architectures-such as linear attention and state-space models, and hybrid designs that combine local and global attention patterns. Models like EAGLE [39], Falcon Mamba [79] and MiniCPM4 [58] demonstrate the scal- ability of purely linear or sparse approaches to the multi-billion parameter scale, offering strong performance with constant-time inference. Meanwhile, hybrid models [5, 26, 28, 33, 54, 57, 67] 3 interleave dense, sparse, and local attention to balance computational efficiency with context modeling capacity, reflecting a growing trend toward compositional, hardware-aware attention designs in modern LLMs. Our goal is to provide a unified framework for understanding the evolution of attention mechanisms under both algorithmic and hardware constraints, and how these designs are integrated into scalable LLM architectures. By connecting theoretical insights with practical im- plementations, we hope this survey offers a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners working toward efficient and deployable model design. This survey is motivated by a pivotal transition in the landscape of Large Language Models. While previous development was predominantly driven by a parameter-scaling paradigm aimed at maximizing capability, the current frontier has shifted toward an efficiency-centric orientation. As demands for million-token contexts and low inference cost, the quadratic time-space complexity of canonical self-attention constitutes the principal bottleneck inhibiting scalability. Consequently, the redesign of attention mechanisms has emerged as the critical frontier for architectural innovation. Synthesizing these developments is essential to bridge the disconnect between theoretical algorithmic design and the practical latencies imposed by modern hardware accelerators, thereby laying the groundwork for the next generation of scalable and commercially viable models. YOCO [54] and Phi-4-mini-flash [48] adopt a dual-decoder architecture that separates the prefill and generation phases. The Self-Decoder utilizes linear attention mechanisms such as RetNet and Sliding-Window Attention for both prefill and generation, while the Cross-Decoder is activated only during generation. TAKEAWAYS Based on the current trajectory of both academic research and industrial deployment, several key consensus points emerge regarding the design of efficient attention mechanisms. The Superiority of HybridityThere is a growing consensus that while purely linear attention architectures offer impressive inference speeds, they frequently incur a non-trivial performance penalty in complex reasoning and ultra-long context retrieval. Consequently, hybrid models have emerged as the preferred architecture. These designs not only maintain the near-lossless performance of standard Transformers but demonstrate the potential to exceed them by balanc- ing global associative memory with precise local retrieval. The Gradient Bottleneck in sharing mecha- nism enables efficient long-context processing with reduced memory and latency overhead. YOCO [54] and Phi-4-mini-flash [48] adopt a dual-decoder architecture that separates the prefill and generation phases. The Self-Decoder utilizes linear attention mechanisms such as RetNet and Sliding-Window Attention for both prefill and generation, while the Cross-Decoder is activated only during generation. A single-layer global KV cache is used throughout, allowing linear-time prefill and efficient decoding with minimal GPU memory consumption. 19 In summary, these recent advances underscore the trend toward hybridizing attention mechanisms to achieve balanced performance across varying computational constraints and sequence lengths. Each architecture uniquely contributes insights into effectively combining local detail management with global context integration, thereby providing valuable frameworks for future attention mechanism developments. 5. TAKEAWAYS Based on the current trajectory of both academic research and industrial deployment, several key consensus points emerge regarding the design of efficient attention mechanisms. The Superiority of HybridityThere is a growing consensus that while purely linear attention architectures offer impressive inference speeds, they frequently incur a non-trivial performance penalty in complex reasoning and ultra-long context retrieval. Consequently, hybrid models have emerged as the preferred architecture. These designs not only maintain the near-lossless performance of standard Transformers but demonstrate the potential to exceed them by balanc- ing global associative memory with precise local retrieval. The Gradient Bottleneck in Sparse TrainingTraining sparse attention models from scratch remains significantly more challenging than dense counterparts. This performance gap primarily stems from gradient sparsity, where restricted connectivity leads to suboptimal optimization dynamics and lower learning efficiency. While self-distillation has shown promise in bridging this gap, it remains an auxiliary solution, indicating that sparse-from-scratch strategies require further foundational innovation. Complementary Strengths of Linear and Sparse AttentionFrom a unified functional per- spective, linear and sparse mechanisms are increasingly viewed as complementary rather than competitive. In a modern efficient stack, linear attention serves as an effective state compressor for fast inference and KV cache reduction, while sparse attention acts as a high-fidelity module to replace full attention during decoding. A robust architecture leverages this synergy to navigate the Pareto frontier of computational throughput and predictive accuracy. The Critical Role of Hardware-Algorithm Co-designA recurring takeaway is that theoretical FLOPs reduction does not inherently translate to wall-clock speedups. Modern efficient attention is inextricably bound to hardware optimization. For instance, the utility of linear attention hinges on switching between recurrent and parallel forms based on the workload, while sparse attention's success depends on resolving the tension between theoretical sparsity and the massive parallelism required by modern GPUs. 6. Outlook This survey presents a comprehensive overview of efficient attention mechanisms, focusing on their algorithmic foundations, practical implementations, and integration into large-scale pre-trained language models. By categorizing linear and sparse attention into well-defined paradigms, we identify key design principles that enable scalability, computational efficiency, 20 and long-context capability. We also analyze how these mechanisms are deployed in state-of- the-art models, either as standalone architectures or as part of hybrid designs that balance local and global computation. Looking forward, we highlight several key directions that are expected to shape future research in this area: Architectural Understanding of Hybrid ModelsWhile prior work in linear attention has largely focused on standalone linear architectures, hybrid models are often constructed by combining off-the-shelf linear attention modules with dense or local components. However, it remains unclear whether a stronger linear backbone directly translates to improved hybrid performance. Future work should investigate hybrid models as a distinct architectural class, seeking to understand their composition, interaction effects, and optimization dynamics. Lossless Sparse Attention and Extended ContextSparse attention remains challenged by a trade-off between accuracy and computational gain. Fully trained sparse models often under- perform dense ones, while post-training sparse approximations face limitations due to lack of end-to-end training. A major research frontier lies in developing sparse attention mechanisms that maintain the expressiveness and accuracy of dense attention, while scaling to much longer contexts. Additionally, the relationship between sparse budget and context length is poorly understood, where fixed top-k schemes may degrade with longer sequences, calling for more adaptive strategies. Mechanistic Insights into Sparse and Hybrid AttentionWhile empirical studies have re- peatedly demonstrated that hybrid attention models can match or exceed dense models using fewer attention computations, the underlying reasons for this effectiveness remain insufficiently explored. Besides, it is especially important to investigate whether the sparsity patterns that work well in synthetic benchmarks generalize to real-world tasks, and to characterize the limits of sparsity-based generalization. As attention-based models continue to evolve, we expect further convergence between architectural innovation, theoretical insight, and hardware-aware design. We hope this sur- vey provides a solid foundation for future research into efficient, high-performance language modeling systems. 21 References 1 Maximilian Beck, Korbinian Pöppel, Markus Spanring, Andreas Auer, Oleksandra Prud- nikova, Michael Kopp, Günter Klambauer, Johannes Brandstetter, and Sepp Hochreiter. xLSTM: Extended long short-term memory.arXiv preprint arXiv:2405.04517, 2024. 2 Ali Behrouz, Zeman Li, Praneeth Kacham, Majid Daliri, Yuan Deng, Peilin Zhong, Meisam Razaviyayn, and Vahab Mirrokni. Rd, such as a hidden layer in a typical sequence transduction encoder or decoder. Motivating our use of self-attention we consider three desiderata. One is the total computational complexity per layer. Another is the amount of computation that can be parallelized, as measured by the minimum number of sequential operations required. The third is the path length between long-range dependencies in the network. Learning long-range dependencies is a key challenge in many sequence transduction tasks. One key factor affecting the ability to learn such dependencies is the length of the paths forward and backward signals have to traverse in the network. The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies [12]. Hence we also compare the maximum path length between any two input and output positions in networks composed of the different layer types. As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations. In terms of computational complexity, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence 6 length n is smaller than the representation dimensionality d, which is most often the case with sentence representations used by state-of-the-art models in machine translations, such as word-piece [38] and byte-pair [31] representations. To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r in the input sequence centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to O(n/r). We plan to investigate this approach further in future work. School of Mathematical Sciences University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Editor: My editor Abstract Attention mechanism has been extensively integrated within mainstream neural network architectures, such as Transformers and graph attention networks. Yet, its underlying working principles remain somewhat elusive. What is its essence? Are there any connec- tions between it and traditional machine learning algorithms? In this study, we inspect the process of computing similarity using classic metrics and vector space properties in manifold learning, clustering, and supervised learning. We identify the key characteristics of similarity computation and information propagation in these methods and demonstrate that the self-attention mechanism in deep learning adheres to the same principles but op- erates more flexibly and adaptively. We decompose the self-attention mechanism into a learnable pseudo-metric function and an information propagation process based on similar- ity computation. We prove that the self-attention mechanism converges to a drift-diffusion process through continuous modeling provided the pseudo-metric is a transformation of a metric and certain reasonable assumptions hold. This equation could be transformed into a heat equation under a new metric. In addition, we give a first-order analysis of attention mechanism with a general pseudo-metric function. This study aids in understanding the effects and principle of attention mechanism through physical intuition. Finally, we pro- pose a modified attention mechanism called metric-attention by leveraging the concept of metric learning to facilitate the ability to learn desired metrics more effectively. Experi- mental results demonstrate that it outperforms self-attention regarding training efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.
