This capability is particularly critical for handling inputs where the lengths and relevance strengths of different parts can vary significantly. As a result, this mechanism contributes to the broad applications of deep learning in various fields, including natural language processing (Devlin et al., 2018; Brown et al., 2020; Radford et al., 2019), computer vision (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2021; Carion et al., 2020), graph mining (Liu et al., 2023) and bioinformatics (Dong and Zhang, 2022; Zhang et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2021). However, understanding the mathematical principle of attention mechanism is still chal- lenging due to its interaction with normalization layers and feed-forward networks in neural network architectures. Difficulties in understanding attention mechanism also stem from the numerous parameters in neural networks and various engineering techniques. To our knowledge, only a few studies have explored it in depth (Vuckovic et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2021; Sander et al., 2022; Geshkovski et al., 2023). Sander et al. (2022) formalized the self-attention mechanism with residual connections as a flow map and analyzed it from the perspective of the Wasserstein gradient flow. In addition, they characterized the L2 self- attention (Kim et al., 2021) using continuous dynamical systems. Geshkovski et al. (2023) investigated attention mechanism in Transformers by assuming that data is distributed on the unit sphere and making simplified assumptions about parameters and proved that the distribution would converge to a single point under certain conditions, suggesting that at- tention mechanism induces an aggregation tendency. However, they did not fully explain how attention mechanism works or its connection to classical algorithms. Moreover, several architectures, such as CRATE (Yu et al., 2024) and Probabilistic Transformer (Wu and Tu, 2023), have been proposed. They often originate from inter- pretable models and have information propagation mechanisms similar to attention mecha- nism. While not strictly equivalent, they offer valuable insights into understanding attention mechanism. For example, CRATE suggests that attention mechanism functions as a com- pression process, whereas the Probabilistic Transformer explains it as an explicit iteration of the Frank-Wolfe optimization algorithm. We illustrate three architecture components, i.e., the residual block, the attention block, and their recombination of a Transformer block (Figure 1). The attention block consists of an information propagation process followed by a linear transformation. Some studies modeled the residual block using an ordinary differential equation (E, 2017; Chen et al., 2018). Some researchers modeled the recombination of the residual and attention blocks using the flow map mentioned above. In this paper, we focus on the attention-based in- formation propagation mechanism. This mechanism can be viewed as a message-passing process akin to that in graph neural networks (GNNs) operating on fully connected graphs. However, GNNs typically employ fixed edge weights and topologies, which limit theoretical analysis to diffusion processes on graphs (Li et al., 2024). In contrast, attention mechanism, as a learnable method of information propagation on fully connected graphs, has yet to be thoroughly analyzed in terms of its limit behavior. Many machine learning methods such as manifold learning (e.g., diffusion map (Coif- man and Lafon, 2006), UMAP (McInnes et al., 2018)), clustering methods (e.g., k-means clustering (Lloyd, 1982), fuzzy c-means clustering (Bezdek et al., 1984), Markov cluster- ing (Van Dongen, 2008)) and supervised learning (e.g., k-nearest neighbors algorithm (Fix, 2 Towards Understanding how attention mechanism works in deep learning 1985), support vector machine (Cortes and Vapnik, 1995)), involve computing similarity or dissimilarity for pairwise data points (or nodes in a graph). These approaches usually consist of some of the following components successively: (1) Initializing similarity based on the input data and the adopted pseudo-metric; (2) Strengthening similarity through some transformation to make similar data points more similar or dissimilar ones more distinct; (3) Normalizing similarity to transform the similarity matrix into a type of probability distribution, which allows the use of probabilistic tools for comparison or further manipu- lation. Traditional algorithms aim to compute similarity by combining classic metrics and handcrafted designs to capture data features or extract information. Figure 1: Illustration of three ar- chitecture components in- cluding the residual block (A), the attention block (C), and their recombina- tion (B) of a Transformer block. We can intuitively observe that attention mech- anism also follows this principle of similarity com- putation to capture the inherent patterns in data. In this study, by exploring the common approach of similarity computation in classic machine learn- ing algorithms, we explain how this technique is uti- lized in attention mechanism, thereby revealing its connections to classical machine learning algorithms. In addition, we illustrate that under certain assump- tions like (1) the formulation of similarity can be de- composed into a transformation of a learnable met- ric function, a parameter on time scale and a soft- max similarity computation; (2) the time-scale pa- rameter is sufficiently small and (3) the manifold hy- pothesis holds, and there are sufficient data points sampled i.i.d. from a continuous distribution, at- tention mechanism for information propagation can be approximated by a drift-diffusion process on the manifold. Furthermore, we prove that, under certain assumptions, this process can be reformalized as a heat diffusion process under a new metric. This pro- vides theoretical support for intuitively understand- ing the working principle of the self-attention mech- anism through physical intuition (Figure 2). In assumption (1), if the learnable function is a general function rather than a metric function, we can still give a first-order analysis to describe the information propagation process of attention mecha- nism. Although this process does not generally cor- respond to a continuous dynamical system, it retains a similar interpretation to the metric version. That is to say, the zeroth-order effect is determined by the nearest data points, while the first- order effect relates to a drift-diffusion process at these points. The main difference between the two lies in how the nearest data points are defined. From the perspective of similarity computation, we decompose the self-attention mecha- nism into an information propagation process based on handcrafted similarity computation 3 Tianyu Ruan and Shihua Zhang and a learnable pseudo-metric. Inspired by this, we propose a modified attention mechanism by leveraging the concept of metric learning to enhance the ability to learn desired metrics more effectively. We refer to this modified attention mechanism as 'metric-attention'. Figure 2: Illustration of the main idea. (a) Attention mechanism consists of two main steps: (1) computing the similarity between nodes (data points or tokens), followed by propagating node features to neighboring nodes, weighted by the similarities, and (2) updating the features of the nodes. (b) Illustration of a drift-diffusion process on the manifold where data reside. This process is driven by two main forces: density guidance, which encourages local concentration, and diffusion, which promotes global consistency of features. This study demonstrates that attention mechanism can be considered a first-order approximation of the drift- diffusion process on manifold, i.e., the short-time diffusion. In Section 2, we introduce the typical techniques of similarity computation used in many classic machine learning algorithms and clarify that attention mechanism also follows this principle. Additionally, we introduce the heat kernel approximation as it relates to atten- tion mechanism. In Section 3, we explore the limit properties of attention mechanism for information propagation and prove that it can be regarded as a first-order approximation of a drift-diffusion equation under certain conditions, which can be further transformed into a heat equation. We also introduce a first-order analysis of information propagation in a generalized pseudo-metric setting. In Section 4, by interpreting attention mechanism as a combination of information propagation based on similarity computation and a learnable pseudo-metric, we propose a metric-attention mechanism to improve information propa- 4 Towards Understanding how attention mechanism works in deep learning gation. Numerical experiments demonstrate its superior performance to the self-attention mechanism on various examples. Finally, we conclude this work and discuss its implications. 2 From similarity computation to attention mechanism 2.1 Similarity computation Similarity computation is a set of engineering practices to generate similarity measures between data points (or graph nodes). Different methods for similarity computation have been developed. Tsinghua University Abstract Transformer-based architectures have become the prevailing backbone of large language models. However, the quadratic time and memory complexity of self-attention remains a fundamental obstacle to efficient long-context modeling. To address this limitation, recent research has introduced two principal categories of efficient attention mechanisms. Linear attention methods achieve linear complexity through kernel approximations, recurrent formulations, or fast- weight dynamics, thereby enabling scalable inference with reduced computational overhead. Sparse attention techniques, in contrast, limit attention computation to selected subsets of tokens based on fixed patterns, block-wise routing, or clustering strategies, enhancing efficiency while preserving contextual coverage. This survey provides a systematic and comprehensive overview of these developments, integrating both algorithmic innovations and hardware-level considerations. In addition, we analyze the incorporation of efficient attention into large- scale pre-trained language models, including both architectures built entirely on efficient attention and hybrid designs that combine local and global components. By aligning theoretical foundations with practical deployment strategies, this work aims to serve as a foundational reference for advancing the design of scalable and efficient language models. Introduction Transformer-based architectures [61] have become the de-facto choice as the backbone of modern Large Language Models (LLMs). Despite their success, the standard self-attention mechanism remains a significant computational bottleneck, with quadratic time and memory complexity with respect to input sequence length. This limitation poses substantial challenges for scaling LLMs to handle increasingly long contexts with both strong performance and high efficiency. To address this, two major directions have emerged to reduce the time and space complexity of softmax Attention. The first mechanism is Linear Attention [17, 22, 50, 53, 70, 72], which seeks to reduce attention complexity by reparameterizing or approximating the softmax attention as linear operations. The second candidate is Sparse Attention [ 8, 21, 34, 56, 73], which restricts attention computation to a subset of the full key space based on fixed or dynamic sparsity pat- terns. While both approaches aim to improve efficiency, they differ significantly in formulation, design choices, and hardware implications. This survey provides a comprehensive review of recent developments in Efficient Attention mechanisms, with a dual focus on algorithmic principles and system-level implementation. Based on that, we also study the Pre-trained LLM employing these Efficient Attentions. We categorize linear attention methods into three major paradigms. First, kernelized linear attention approximates the softmax kernel with inner products in a feature space, achieving linear complexity via random feature maps [ 9, 42] or fixed positive mappings [ 22]. Second, recurrent linear attention with forgetting mechanisms introduces position-aware recurrence, enabling long-sequence modeling through data-independent [53] or data-dependent decay [17, 70], which control how past information fades over time. Third, fast-weight and meta-learning- based formulations reinterpret linear attention as a memory update process optimized online, where models such as DeltaNet [50, 72] and TTT [51, 52] incorporate fast-learning dynamics directly into the state evolution. We also examine hardware-friendly representations of linear attention-including parallel, recurrent, and chunkwise forms-highlighting their respective trade-offs in computational complexity, memory footprint, and compatibility with training or inference workflows. We classify Sparse Attention into fixed-pattern sparsity, block sparsity, and clustering-based sparsity. Fixed-pattern sparsity adopts static token-level masks such as sliding windows, dilated positions, or designated global tokens, offering simplicity and hardware-friendliness [4, 8, 14, 65]. Block sparsity selects or routes attention at block granularity, either via heuristic scoring [34, 56, 66], trainable gating [15, 73], enabling structured memory access and efficient GPU utilization. Clustering-based sparsity organizes key-value pairs using content-based or position-aware grouping methods such as k-means or Local Sensitive Hashing (LSH), facilitating semantically aware retrieval with reduced memory overhead [7, 24, 32]. Finally, we also discuss bidirectional sparse designs extend sparsity patterns to encoder-style models. These approaches differ in sparsity granularity, selection mechanism, and their alignment with hardware primitives like FlashAttention [10], and collectively represent the foundation for efficient long-context modeling in modern Transformers. There are recent efforts to integrate efficient attention mechanisms into industry-level Pre- trained Language Models. These include both pure efficient architectures-such as linear attention and state-space models, and hybrid designs that combine local and global attention patterns. Models like EAGLE [39], Falcon Mamba [79] and MiniCPM4 [58] demonstrate the scal- ability of purely linear or sparse approaches to the multi-billion parameter scale, offering strong performance with constant-time inference. Meanwhile, hybrid models [5, 26, 28, 33, 54, 57, 67] 3 interleave dense, sparse, and local attention to balance computational efficiency with context modeling capacity, reflecting a growing trend toward compositional, hardware-aware attention designs in modern LLMs. Our goal is to provide a unified framework for understanding the evolution of attention mechanisms under both algorithmic and hardware constraints, and how these designs are integrated into scalable LLM architectures. By connecting theoretical insights with practical im- plementations, we hope this survey offers a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners working toward efficient and deployable model design. This survey is motivated by a pivotal transition in the landscape of Large Language Models. While previous development was predominantly driven by a parameter-scaling paradigm aimed at maximizing capability, the current frontier has shifted toward an efficiency-centric orientation. As demands for million-token contexts and low inference cost, the quadratic time-space complexity of canonical self-attention constitutes the principal bottleneck inhibiting scalability. Consequently, the redesign of attention mechanisms has emerged as the critical frontier for architectural innovation. Synthesizing these developments is essential to bridge the disconnect between theoretical algorithmic design and the practical latencies imposed by modern hardware accelerators, thereby laying the groundwork for the next generation of scalable and commercially viable models. To structure this survey, we organize the discussion as follows: ? Section 2 introduces Linear Attention, covering its evolution across different model gener- ations, the associated design principles, and implications for hardware implementation. ? Section 3 presents Sparse Attention, categorizing sparsity patterns, analyzing deployment scenarios, and offering practical system-level design recommendations. ? Section 4 reviews Pre-trained Language Models that incorporate efficient attention mech- anisms, including both uniform efficient architectures and hybrid models that integrate local, sparse, and dense attention. ? Section 5 and 6 offers Takeaways and an Outlook on future directions, discussing open challenges and potential advances in algorithmic and hardware-aligned research. 2. Linear Attention 2.1. Theoretical analysis In this section, we analyze the theoretical properties of Contextual Priority Attention, particularly its relationship to standard self-attention and its capacity to model dependencies in sequential data. Relationship to standard self-attention Standard self-attention computes attention weights as: 12 where are the query and key vectors for tokens i and j, respectively. We can show that under certain conditions, CPA approximates this pairwise attention mechanism. Specifically, if our priority scoring function is structured as: 13 where is a weighted sum of all key vectors (our Global Context Vector), then CPA implicitly captures pairwise interactions through this shared context. Proposition 1 Let be the attention matrix from standard self-attention, and let be the attention weights from CPA. If the GCV is computed as with weights proportional to the importance of token j in the sequence, then there exists a parameterization of the priority scoring function such that 14 The proof is provided in Appendix . The key insight is that CPA's prioritization based on global context provides an efficient proxy for explicit token-to-token attention when the context sufficiently represents the relevant aspects of all tokens. Expressive power A natural question is whether CPA can express the same functions as standard self-attention. We prove that: Theorem 1 For any self-attention mechanism with weights , there exists a parameterization of CPA that can approximate the function computed by this self-attention mechanism to arbitrary precision, provided the dimension of the Global Context Vector is sufficiently large. The proof, outlined in Appendix, relies on the universal approximation capabilities of neural networks30 and the fact that our priority scoring MLP can learn to extract token-specific queries from the global context. With sufficient capacity, the priority scoring function can learn to attend to the same tokens that would receive high attention weights in the standard mechanism. Practical implementation: While Theorem 1 is an existence proof establishing that CPA can theoretically approximate standard attention with a sufficiently large GCV, in our experiments we use a GCV of dimension (i.e., the same as the model dimension). This choice: Does not grow with sequence length n, maintaining constant parameter count Matches the dimensionality of keys and queries in standard Transformers Empirically provides sufficient representational capacity for all tested tasks (section "Results and analysis") The theorem's "sufficient capacity" condition is satisfied by the MLP's hidden dimension ( in our experiments) rather than by increasing the GCV dimension. We found no benefit from using even for sequences up to 32K tokens. While this theoretical result establishes that CPA has the expressive capacity to approximate standard attention, in practice, the inductive biases of the two approaches differ significantly, leading to different learning dynamics and generalization properties. Complexity-expressivity tradeoff We analyze the tradeoff between computational complexity and model expressivity for different attention variants: Standard self-attention: complexity, full expressivity. Linear attention (e.g., Performers): complexity, reduced expressivity due to kernel approximation. Pattern-based sparse attention: complexity where , limited by fixed patterns. CPA (our approach): theoretical complexity with experimentally observed linear scaling, expressivity modulated by GCV capacity. Figure 4 visualizes this tradeoff for various attention mechanisms. Unlike kernel-based methods, CPA doesn't rely on specific mathematical properties of the attention function. Instead, it learns to extract and use relevant global context, potentially capturing higher-order interactions that aren't easily expressible with fixed kernels. Fig. 4. Open in a new tab Theoretical trade-off between computational complexity and expressivity for different attention mechanisms. The arrow indicates the ideal direction (lower complexity, higher expressivity). CPA achieves a favorable balance by maintaining linear complexity while preserving much of the expressivity of standard attention. Information bottleneck perspective The Global Context Vector in CPA can be viewed through the lens of the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle25. The GCV creates a compressed representation of the input sequence, retaining the most relevant information while discarding noise. Proposition 2 Under the Information Bottleneck framework, the optimal Global Context Vector is one that maximizes , where denotes mutual information, is the input sequence, Y is the target output, and controls the compression-relevance tradeoff. This perspective provides theoretical justification for why CPA works well: it implicitly performs a form of information bottleneck, focusing on the most task-relevant aspects of the input sequence while filtering out irrelevant details. Experimental setup We evaluate CPA on a diverse set of tasks to assess its performance across different domains and sequence lengths. Our evaluation focuses on comparing CPA against standard self-attention and state-of-the-art efficient attention mechanisms. Model configurations CPA application in different architectures For encoder-decoder tasks (machine translation, summarization), we apply CPA to replace self-attention in the encoder only. The decoder employs standard masked self-attention for auto-regressive generation and standard cross-attention to attend to encoder outputs. This design choice offers several advantages: The encoder's Global Context Vector is computed once for the entire source sequence and remains fixed during decoding, ensuring efficient inference. The decoder's standard attention preserves the ability to attend to all previously generated tokens without modification. Cross-attention maintains full expressivity for encoder-decoder alignment. For encoder-only tasks (classification, language modeling with fixed context), CPA replaces all self-attention layers. For all model variants, we keep other components (feed-forward networks, layer normalization, residual connections) unchanged. Developing an efficient causal variant of CPA for decoder-only auto-regressive models is a promising direction for future work, which we discuss in section "Future directions". For fair comparison, we maintain the same model size (number of parameters) across all compared models by appropriately adjusting the hidden dimensions. We consider four variants of our approach: CPA-Avg: Using learned weighted averaging for GCV CPA-CLS: Using a [CLS] token approach for GCV CPA-CNN: Using a convolutional network with global pooling for GCV CPA-BERT: A BERT-style model with CPA replacing self-attention For all CPA variants, we use the two-layer MLP priority scoring function with hidden dimension , and the sparsemax transformation for sparse attention allocation unless otherwise specified. Baselines We compare against the following baselines: Standard Transformer1: The original Transformer with full self-attention Sparse Transformer2: Uses fixed sparse attention patterns Longformer8: Combines local windowed attention with global tokens Linformer4: Uses low-rank approximation of attention Performer5: Uses kernel-based approximation Reformer3: Uses locality-sensitive hashing BigBird10: Combines random, global, and local attention patterns We use the official implementations of these baselines with their recommended configurations, adjusting model sizes to match parameter counts for fair comparison. Tasks and datasets We evaluate on the following tasks and datasets: Machine translation: WMT14 English-German (En-De): 4.5M sentence pairs, evaluated with BLEU score WMT14 English-French (En-Fr): 36M sentence pairs, evaluated with BLEU score Language modeling: WikiText-10331: 103M tokens from Wikipedia articles, evaluated with perplexity PG1932: 28K books from Project Gutenberg, evaluated with perplexity Long document classification: Long Range Arena (LRA) benchmark33: A suite of tasks designed to test the ability to handle long-range dependencies IMDB Movie Reviews34: 50K movie reviews for sentiment analysis Hyperpartisan News Detection35: Articles labeled as hyperpartisan or not Question answering: SQuAD v1.1 and v2.036,37: Stanford Question Answering Dataset Natural Questions (NQ)38: Questions from real Google search queries TriviaQA39: Question-answer pairs from trivia competitions Long-context generation: CNN/Daily Mail summarization40: News articles with abstractive summaries arXiv paper summarization41: Scientific papers with abstracts as summaries Implementation details Our implementation is based on PyTorch42 and the HuggingFace Transformers library43. The sparse transformations (sparsemax and top-k Gumbel-Softmax) are implemented using custom CUDA kernels for efficiency. We employ mixed-precision training using NVIDIA Apex for all experiments. For machine translation tasks, we follow the standard Transformer base configuration1 with 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers, 8 attention heads, and 512-dimensional embeddings. For other tasks, we adjust model size according to task complexity and dataset size, ensuring fair comparison across all models. Detailed model configurations for each task are provided in Appendix. Training details We train all models using the Adam optimizer44 with a transformer-standard learning rate schedule: 15 We use label smoothing of 0.1 for classification tasks and dropout with probability 0.1 for all layers. Models are trained on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs with mixed precision training. For each task, we select hyperparameters based on validation performance. We employ early stopping based on validation performance with a patience of 10 epochs. To ensure reproducibility, we use five different random seeds for each experiment and report the mean and standard deviation of the results. Evaluation metrics We use task-specific evaluation metrics: BLEU scores for machine translation, computed using SacreBLEU451 to ensure reproducibility and fair comparison with prior work Perplexity for language modeling Accuracy for classification tasks F1 and Exact Match scores for question answering ROUGE scores (R-1, R-2, R-L) for summarization Additionally, we measure: Training time (hours) Peak memory usage (GB) Inference speed (tokens/second) FLOPs per sequence Model parameter count All runtime and memory measurements are conducted on identical hardware configurations to ensure fair comparison. Results and analysis Performance across tasks Table 2 presents the main results across all tasks, comparing CPA variants with baseline models. For brevity, we report results for the best-performing CPA variant (CPA-Avg) in the main table and provide detailed comparisons between all CPA variants in Appendix. Table 2. Our findings indicate that CPA achieves competitive performance with standard Transformers across all tasks, with performance differences generally within 0.5 points. Among efficient attention variants, CPA-Avg consistently achieves strong results, ranking as first or second-best among efficient attention methods on all benchmarks. On tasks involving long sequences (LRA benchmark and document summarization), CPA demonstrates particularly strong results, outperforming most efficient attention alternatives by a significant margin. This suggests that our global-context approach effectively captures long-range dependencies without requiring quadratic computation. Each path represents a promising avenue for research, with estimated complexity and potential impact. Conclusion We presented Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), a novel attention mechanism that achieves theoretical complexity while empirically demonstrating linear scaling and maintaining competitive performance with standard Transformers. By reimagining attention as a global-context-driven priority system rather than exhaustive pairwise comparisons, CPA offers significant efficiency improvements, particularly for long sequences. Our experimental results across diverse tasks demonstrate that CPA achieves performance comparable to full attention while scaling more efficiently to long inputs. The emergent attention patterns reveal that CPA learns meaningful prioritization strategies that adapt to input complexity. On the Long Range Arena benchmark specifically designed to test long-range modeling capabilities, CPA outperforms other efficient attention variants by a significant margin. The success of CPA suggests that the quadratic computational complexity of standard self-attention may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. By focusing computational resources on the most contextually relevant tokens, CPA provides an efficient alternative that scales better to the increasingly long contexts required by modern NLP applications. The ability to process sequences of tens of thousands of tokens efficiently opens up new possibilities for applications such as document-level translation, long-form question answering, and full-document summarization. Conclusion We presented Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), a novel attention mechanism that achieves theoretical complexity while empirically demonstrating linear scaling and maintaining competitive performance with standard Transformers. By reimagining attention as a global-context-driven priority system rather than exhaustive pairwise comparisons, CPA offers significant efficiency improvements, particularly for long sequences. Our experimental results across diverse tasks demonstrate that CPA achieves performance comparable to full attention while scaling more efficiently to long inputs. The emergent attention patterns reveal that CPA learns meaningful prioritization strategies that adapt to input complexity. On the Long Range Arena benchmark specifically designed to test long-range modeling capabilities, CPA outperforms other efficient attention variants by a significant margin. The success of CPA suggests that the quadratic computational complexity of standard self-attention may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. By focusing computational resources on the most contextually relevant tokens, CPA provides an efficient alternative that scales better to the increasingly long contexts required by modern NLP applications. The ability to process sequences of tens of thousands of tokens efficiently opens up new possibilities for applications such as document-level translation, long-form question answering, and full-document summarization. As models continue to scale and applications demand increasingly longer context windows, approaches like CPA that break the quadratic scaling barrier without significant performance degradation will become increasingly important. We believe this work represents an important step toward more efficient transformer architectures and hope that the global-context approach inspires further innovations in attention mechanisms. Future work will explore hierarchical extensions of CPA, dynamic sparsity approaches, and applications to multimodal tasks, further extending the capabilities of this promising approach. Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.18288v1 URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.18288v1 Task: q001 Submitted month/day; Revised x/x; Published x/x Towards understanding how attention mechanism works in deep learning Tianyu Ruan? ? ruantianyu17@mails.ucas.ac.cn Shihua Zhang? ? zsh@amss.ac.cn ? Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science Chinese Academy of Sciences ? School of Mathematical Sciences University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Editor: My editor Abstract Attention mechanism has been extensively integrated within mainstream neural network architectures, such as Transformers and graph attention networks. Yet, its underlying working principles remain somewhat elusive. What is its essence? Are there any connec- tions between it and traditional machine learning algorithms? In this study, we inspect the process of computing similarity using classic metrics and vector space properties in manifold learning, clustering, and supervised learning. We identify the key characteristics of similarity computation and information propagation in these methods and demonstrate that the self-attention mechanism in deep learning adheres to the same principles but op- erates more flexibly and adaptively. We decompose the self-attention mechanism into a learnable pseudo-metric function and an information propagation process based on similar- ity computation. We prove that the self-attention mechanism converges to a drift-diffusion process through continuous modeling provided the pseudo-metric is a transformation of a metric and certain reasonable assumptions hold. This equation could be transformed into a heat equation under a new metric. In addition, we give a first-order analysis of attention mechanism with a general pseudo-metric function. This study aids in understanding the effects and principle of attention mechanism through physical intuition. Finally, we pro- pose a modified attention mechanism called metric-attention by leveraging the concept of metric learning to facilitate the ability to learn desired metrics more effectively. Experi- mental results demonstrate that it outperforms self-attention regarding training efficiency, accuracy, and robustness. Keywords Attention mechanism, Transformer, graph attention network, similarity computation, heat diffusion 1 Introduction The attention or self-attention mechanism is extensively applied in popular deep learning architectures like Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2018) and graph attention networks (Veli? ckovi´ c et al., 2017). This mechanism enables the model to assign diverse ©2024 Tianyu Ruan and Shihua Zhang. License: CC-BY 4.0, seehttps://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Attribution requirements are provided at http://jmlr.org/papers/v23/21-0000.html. arXiv:2412.18288v1 [cs.LG] 24 Dec 2024 Tianyu Ruan and Shihua Zhang weights to various parts (data points, nodes, etc.) of the input sequence (data, graph, etc.) based on their relevance when producing an output. This capability is particularly critical for handling inputs where the lengths and relevance strengths of different parts can vary significantly. As a result, this mechanism contributes to the broad applications of deep learning in various fields, including natural language processing (Devlin et al., 2018; Brown et al., 2020; Radford et al., 2019), computer vision (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2021; Carion et al., 2020), graph mining (Liu et al., 2023) and bioinformatics (Dong and Zhang, 2022; Zhang et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2021). However, understanding the mathematical principle of attention mechanism is still chal- lenging due to its interaction with normalization layers and feed-forward networks in neural network architectures. Difficulties in understanding attention mechanism also stem from the numerous parameters in neural networks and various engineering techniques. To our knowledge, only a few studies have explored it in depth (Vuckovic et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2021; Sander et al., 2022; Geshkovski et al., 2023). Sander et al. (2022) formalized the self-attention mechanism with residual connections as a flow map and analyzed it from the perspective of the Wasserstein gradient flow. In addition, they characterized the L2 self- attention (Kim et al., 2021) using continuous dynamical systems. Geshkovski et al. (2023) investigated attention mechanism in Transformers by assuming that data is distributed on the unit sphere and making simplified assumptions about parameters and proved that the distribution would converge to a single point under certain conditions, suggesting that at- tention mechanism induces an aggregation tendency. However, they did not fully explain how attention mechanism works or its connection to classical algorithms. Moreover, several architectures, such as CRATE (Yu et al., 2024) and Probabilistic Transformer (Wu and Tu, 2023), have been proposed. They often originate from inter- pretable models and have information propagation mechanisms similar to attention mecha- nism. While not strictly equivalent, they offer valuable insights into understanding attention mechanism. For example, CRATE suggests that attention mechanism functions as a com- pression process, whereas the Probabilistic Transformer explains it as an explicit iteration of the Frank-Wolfe optimization algorithm. We illustrate three architecture components, i.e., the residual block, the attention block, and their recombination of a Transformer block (Figure 1). The attention block consists of an information propagation process followed by a linear transformation. Some studies modeled the residual block using an ordinary differential equation (E, 2017; Chen et al., 2018). Some researchers modeled the recombination of the residual and attention blocks using the flow map mentioned above. In this paper, we focus on the attention-based in- formation propagation mechanism. This mechanism can be viewed as a message-passing process akin to that in graph neural networks (GNNs) operating on fully connected graphs. However, GNNs typically employ fixed edge weights and topologies, which limit theoretical analysis to diffusion processes on graphs (Li et al., 2024). In contrast, attention mechanism, as a learnable method of information propagation on fully connected graphs, has yet to be thoroughly analyzed in terms of its limit behavior. Many machine learning methods such as manifold learning (e.g., diffusion map (Coif- man and Lafon, 2006), UMAP (McInnes et al., 2018)), clustering methods (e.g., k-means clustering (Lloyd, 1982), fuzzy c-means clustering (Bezdek et al., 1984), Markov cluster- ing (Van Dongen, 2008)) and supervised learning (e.g., k-nearest neighbors algorithm (Fix, 2 Towards Understanding how attention mechanism works in deep learning 1985), support vector machine (Cortes and Vapnik, 1995)), involve computing similarity or dissimilarity for pairwise data points (or nodes in a graph). These approaches usually consist of some of the following components successively: (1) Initializing similarity based on the input data and the adopted pseudo-metric; (2) Strengthening similarity through some transformation to make similar data points more similar or dissimilar ones more distinct; (3) Normalizing similarity to transform the similarity matrix into a type of probability distribution, which allows the use of probabilistic tools for comparison or further manipu- lation. Traditional algorithms aim to compute similarity by combining classic metrics and handcrafted designs to capture data features or extract information. Figure 1: Illustration of three ar- chitecture components in- cluding the residual block (A), the attention block (C), and their recombina- tion (B) of a Transformer block. We can intuitively observe that attention mech- anism also follows this principle of similarity com- putation to capture the inherent patterns in data. In this study, by exploring the common approach of similarity computation in classic machine learn- ing algorithms, we explain how this technique is uti- lized in attention mechanism, thereby revealing its connections to classical machine learning algorithms. In addition, we illustrate that under certain assump- tions like (1) the formulation of similarity can be de- composed into a transformation of a learnable met- ric function, a parameter on time scale and a soft- max similarity computation; (2) the time-scale pa- rameter is sufficiently small and (3) the manifold hy- pothesis holds, and there are sufficient data points sampled i.i.d. from a continuous distribution, at- tention mechanism for information propagation can be approximated by a drift-diffusion process on the manifold. Furthermore, we prove that, under certain assumptions, this process can be reformalized as a heat diffusion process under a new metric. This pro- vides theoretical support for intuitively understand- ing the working principle of the self-attention mech- anism through physical intuition (Figure 2). In assumption (1), if the learnable function is a general function rather than a metric function, we can still give a first-order analysis to describe the information propagation process of attention mecha- nism. Although this process does not generally cor- respond to a continuous dynamical system, it retains a similar interpretation to the metric version. That is to say, the zeroth-order effect is determined by the nearest data points, while the first- order effect relates to a drift-diffusion process at these points. The main difference between the two lies in how the nearest data points are defined. From the perspective of similarity computation, we decompose the self-attention mecha- nism into an information propagation process based on handcrafted similarity computation 3 Tianyu Ruan and Shihua Zhang and a learnable pseudo-metric. Inspired by this, we propose a modified attention mechanism by leveraging the concept of metric learning to enhance the ability to learn desired metrics more effectively. We refer to this modified attention mechanism as 'metric-attention'. Figure 2: Illustration of the main idea. (a) Attention mechanism consists of two main steps: (1) computing the similarity between nodes (data points or tokens), followed by propagating node features to neighboring nodes, weighted by the similarities, and (2) updating the features of the nodes. (b) Illustration of a drift-diffusion process on the manifold where data reside. This process is driven by two main forces: density guidance, which encourages local concentration, and diffusion, which promotes global consistency of features. This study demonstrates that attention mechanism can be considered a first-order approximation of the drift- diffusion process on manifold, i.e., the short-time diffusion. In Section 2, we introduce the typical techniques of similarity computation used in many classic machine learning algorithms and clarify that attention mechanism also follows this principle. Additionally, we introduce the heat kernel approximation as it relates to atten- tion mechanism. In Section 3, we explore the limit properties of attention mechanism for information propagation and prove that it can be regarded as a first-order approximation of a drift-diffusion equation under certain conditions, which can be further transformed into a heat equation. We also introduce a first-order analysis of information propagation in a generalized pseudo-metric setting. In Section 4, by interpreting attention mechanism as a combination of information propagation based on similarity computation and a learnable pseudo-metric, we propose a metric-attention mechanism to improve information propa- 4 Towards Understanding how attention mechanism works in deep learning gation. Numerical experiments demonstrate its superior performance to the self-attention mechanism on various examples. Finally, we conclude this work and discuss its implications. 2 From similarity computation to attention mechanism 2.1 Similarity computation Similarity computation is a set of engineering practices to generate similarity measures between data points (or graph nodes). Different methods for similarity computation have been developed. Most of them involve one, two, or three of the following three components: initializing similarity, strengthening similarity, and normalizing similarity. 2.1.1 Initializing similarity Initializing similarity is the first step for further computations and information extraction. The point-to-point similarity is typically generated using a binary function D(·, ·), where D is often a simple transformation based on metrics, inner products, or topological structures. A natural idea is that the closer two data points are, the higher their similarity. There- fore, the distance between two data points is often transformed into a similarity measure through monotonically decreasing mappings. [All Articles](https://erdem.pl/) # Introduction to Attention Mechanism Published 12 May 2021 · ![15min coffee icon]( coffee icon]( coffee icon]( )![5min coffee icon]( )54 min read The attention mechanism is one of the most important inventions in Machine Learning, at this moment (2021) it's used to achieve impressive results in almost every field of ML, and today I want to explain where it came from and how it works. Before even beginning to explain Attention we have to go back and see the problem which Attention was supposed to solve. Before 2015, there was an issue with RNN which was occurred when the input sequence was really long. x1 We x2 are x3 learning x4 attention **Input**: Sequence x1, ?, xT PrevNext Figure 1: Sequence-to-sequence with RNN, Designed base on [_"Sequence to sequence learning with neural networks"_, NeurIPS 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) Paper, [UMich](https://web.eecs.umich.edu/~justincj/teaching/eecs498/FA2019/) This solution works fine as long as the sentence is short. After the decoder is done with its job, we're left with the **context vector _c_** and the **initial decoder state s0s\_0s0?**. Those two vectors have to _"summarize"_ the whole input sequence because we're going to feed them into the decoder part of our model. You can treat the context vector as something that transferring information between the encoded sequence and the decoded sequence. For long sentences, like **T=100**, it is highly probable that our context vector _**c**_ is not going to be able to hold all meaningful information from the encoded sequence. Consider this quote: > "In a way, AI is both closer and farther off than we imagine. AI is closer to being able to do more powerful things than most people expect - driving cars, curing diseases, discovering planets, understanding media. Those will each have a great impact on the world, but we're still figuring out what real intelligence is." - **Mark Zuckerberg** in _**"Building Jarvis"**_ It is a lot easier to compress the first sentence to the context vector than to do the same for a whole quote. We could create longer and longer context vectors but because RNNs are sequential that won't scale up. That's where the Attention Mechanism comes in. The idea is to create **a new context vector every timestep** of the decoder which attends differently to the encoded sequence. x1 We x2 are x3 learning x4 attention h1 h2 h3 h4 s0 PrevNext Figure 2: Sequence-to-sequence with RNN (with Attention), Designed base on [_"Neural machine transla$on by jointly learning to align and translate"_, NeurIPS 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473) Paper, [UMich](https://web.eecs.umich.edu/~justincj/teaching/eecs498/FA2019/) This time we're computing an additional context vector on every step of the decoder. Let us go through one whole step to explain what is happening. ### [1 compute alignment scores permalink](https://erdem.pl/2021/05/introduction-to-attention-mechanism\#1-compute-alignment-scores) 1\. Compute alignment scores ![alignment scores]( 3: Alignment Scores for **t=1**, [Source: erdem.pl](https://erdem.pl/2021/04/introduction-to-attention-mechanism) At t=1t=1t=1 we're going to use st-1s\_{t-1}st-1? decoder state to computer alignment scores. To compute the alignment score for every encoder state we're using a function that is called _alignment function_ but it's just an MLP (MultiLayer Perceptron). Each alignment score can be treated as "how much h1h\_1h1? is useful in predicting the output in the state s0s\_0s0?". The alignment function outputs a scalar value which is a real number and we cannot use it just like that, we have to normalize those values using the softmax function. ### [2 compute attention weights permalink](https://erdem.pl/2021/05/introduction-to-attention-mechanism\#2-compute-attention-weights) 2\. Compute attention weights ![attention weights]( 4: Attention weights for **t=1**, [Source: erdem.pl](https://erdem.pl/2021/04/introduction-to-attention-mechanism) Output from the softmax function is normalized so all the numbers sum up to 1. Those outputs are called **Attention weights** and as the name says, they show the model "how much it should attend to corresponding hidden state". ### [3 compute context vector permalink](https://erdem.pl/2021/05/introduction-to-attention-mechanism\#3-compute-context-vector) 3\. Compute context vector ![context vector]( 5: Context vector calculation for **t=1**, [Source: erdem.pl](https://erdem.pl/2021/04/introduction-to-attention-mechanism) Now a lot of things happen (3 steps in the diagram above). First, we multiplied every attention weight by corresponding hidden state (a1,1xh1,1a\_{1,1} \\times h\_{1,1}a1,1?xh1,1?, a1,2xh1,2a\_{1,2} \\times h\_{1,2}a1,2?xh1,2??). Then, all of the results are summed to use as a **context vector c1c\_1c1?**. > **Note:** > > You've probably noticed that at this point "context vector" is actually a "context scalar" but this is just because we decided to have only 1D output (easier to show and understand for now). I'm going to switch to vectors when we get to abstracting attention to its own layer. ### [4 compute the first output permalink](https://erdem.pl/2021/05/introduction-to-attention-mechanism\#4-compute-the-first-output) 4\. Compute the first output ![first output]( 6: Decoder's output for **t=1**, [Source: erdem.pl](https://erdem.pl/2021/04/introduction-to-attention-mechanism) At the end of the first timestep, we can finally compute the first output from the decoder. That output is computed using context vector c1c\_1c1?, previous decoder's state s0s\_0s0?, and start token y0y\_0y0?. Interesting thing is that in that whole process we don't have to train fattf\_{att}fatt? as a separate model. The **whole process is differentiable**, so we can just backpropagate through the computational graph. ### [5 and repeat permalink](https://erdem.pl/2021/05/introduction-to-attention-mechanism\#5-and-repeat) 5\. And repeat? ![t 2]( 7: New context vector for **t=2**, [Source: erdem.pl](https://erdem.pl/2021/04/introduction-to-attention-mechanism) At the timestep t=2t=2t=2 only thing we have to do is to **change the input to calculate the alignment scores from s0s\_0s0? to s1s\_1s1?**. Using the same process we compute new scores (e2,1e\_{2,1}e2,1?, e2,1e\_{2,1}e2,1??) and attention weights (a2,1a\_{2,1}a2,1?, a2,1a\_{2,1}a2,1??). Then multiply new attention weights and encoder's hidden states to compute the new context vector c2c\_2c2?. At this point, the whole process just runs in the loop until the decoder produces _\[STOP\]_ token (sometimes called _\[EOS\]_ token, eng. End Of Sentence). ## [attention weights visualization permalink](https://erdem.pl/2021/05/introduction-to-attention-mechanism\#attention-weights-visualization) Attention weights visualization ![attention weights heatmap]( 8: Attention weights for English to French translation, Source: [Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473) In the original paper, there is a simple visualization of the attention weights ai,ja\_{i,j}ai,j? generated when translating the English sentence _"The agreement on the European Economic Area was signed in August 1992."_ into French _"L'accord sur la zone économique européenne a été signé en août 1992."_. This visualization shows us a couple of interesting things. The first thing is a diagonal pattern which tells us that model put more attention to corresponding French word from the same position. The second thing is more interesting and it is the phrase _"European Economic Area"_ which in French has reverse order _"la zone économique européenne"_. We can see that when generating `la` token model puts more attention on `the` and `Area`, then when generating the `zone` token it attends to `Area` and `Economic` (ignoring `European`). Another interesting observation is _"a été signé"_ where when generating `a` and `été` tokens, the model attends to both `was` and `signed` (it makes sense in French because we need to know an exact variation of the word `étre`). This heatmap is important because we didn't tell the model which words it should attend to, it learned this by itself. Additionally, we've got a kind of interpretability of the model's decision. ## [attention doesnt know that input is a sequence permalink](https://erdem.pl/2021/05/introduction-to-attention-mechanism\#attention-doesnt-know-that-input-is-a-sequence) Attention doesn't know that input is a sequence You probably started to worry about what happened with my information from the last step: _"We're not using the fact that h vector is an ordered sequence. It is used as unordered set instead. To solve this we have to add a positional encoding to each element"_ I've written a piece on positional encoding as a separate article because there is too much information to squeeze into this one. If you're interested please check [Understanding Positional Encoding in Transformers](https://erdem.pl/2021/05/understanding-positional-encoding-in-transformers). This is still a thing but instead of solving that problem, make use of it to abstract attention mechanism and use it for something different than a sequence of text. What about describing images with attention? There is a paper from the same year called [_"Show, Attend, and Tell: Neural Image Caption Generation with Visual Attention"_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03044) that uses attention on CNN's embedding to generate image captioning with the help of an RNN decoder. ![orignal_img]( CNN h1,1 h1,2 h1,3 h2,1 h2,2 h2,3 h3,1 h3,2 h3,3 s0 PrevNext Figure 9: Image Captioning with Attention (still RNN), Designed base on [_"Show, Attend, and Tell: Neural Image Caption Generation with Visual Attention"_, ICML 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03044) Paper, [UMich](https://web.eecs.umich.edu/~justincj/teaching/eecs498/FA2019/) In this paper, the authors are proposing a solution based on convolutional feature extraction instead of the standard RNN encoder network. We're using those features from CNN to compute state and then to compute alignment scores for every timestep of the RNN decoder. As in the previous example, I'm going to walk you through the whole process, but you probably are able to understand it base on the interactive diagram above :) ![cnn alignment]( 10: Alignment score calculation from extracted features, [Source: erdem.pl](https://erdem.pl/2021/04/introduction-to-attention-mechanism) We're assuming that CNN is already trained and produces our 3x3 grid. We're going to use that initial grid to predict the initial hidden state s0s\_0s0? (sometimes it could be randomly generated or even set to 0). Now we have to pass the same grid and s0s\_0s0? to the alignment function to calculate corresponding alignment score for each value of the grid et,i,j=fatt(st-1,hi,j)e\_{t,i,j} = f\_{att}(s\_{t-1}, h\_{i,j})et,i,j?=fatt?(st-1?,hi,j?). That gives us alignment scores for **t=1** timestep. As in the previous example, each alignment score is a scalar which tells us "how important is given feature in the current timestep". ![cnn attention weights]( 11: Attention weights, [Source: erdem.pl](https://erdem.pl/2021/04/introduction-to-attention-mechanism) With alignment scores calculated we need to apply softmax to normalize scores to some probability distribution that sums to one. ![cnn attention mask]( 12: Compute context vector and generate first output, [Source: erdem.pl](https://erdem.pl/2021/04/introduction-to-attention-mechanism) Now all we have to do is to compute [Hadamard product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_product_(matrices)) (element-wise multiplication, hi,jxat,i,jh\_{i,j} \\times a\_{t,i,j}hi,j?xat,i,j? ?) and sum everything to get a context vector c1c\_1c1?. The rest works exactly like in the previous example so we use context vector c1c\_1c1?, start token y0y\_0y0?, and initial decoder state s0s\_0s0? and pass it through gUg\_UgU? function to calculate s1s\_1s1? state and achieve some output token y1y\_1y1?. > **Note** > > The sum is not required at this point, I'm just doing it to have the same shape of the context vector as in the previous example. We could easily use a 3x3 matrix as an input to the gUg\_UgU? function. ![cnn second timestep]( 14: Second timestep ( **t=2**), [Source: erdem.pl](https://erdem.pl/2021/04/introduction-to-attention-mechanism) The same as before, we're using newly generated s1s\_1s1? state to compute new alignment scores e2,i,je\_{2,i,j}e2,i,j?, which then are normalized with softmax and computed into context vector c2c\_2c2?. The process stops when the decoder produces _\[STOP\]_ token as an output. ## [visualization of the attention weights permalink](https://erdem.pl/2021/05/introduction-to-attention-mechanism\#visualization-of-the-attention-weights) Visualization of the attention weights The same as in sequence to sequence translation we are able to visualize attention weights in this case. I'm going to use one of the examples provided by the authors. ![show attend soft example]( 15: Image attention visualization, white regions have higher value of the attention weight, Source: [Show, Attend, and Tell: Neural Image Caption Generation with Visual Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03044) As you can see this is not an ideal solution for explaining a model but still could give you a kind of intuition about what is happening. Especially when we look at the tokens like `frisbee` or `park` when the model attends to those exact objects. In the case of the token `woman`, both people on the image save similar attention weights but that's still ok because the model could decide which one is the subject and how to name that person. There is one more type of attention called **hard attention** where instead of using the softmax function, we're selecting a feature with the highest alignment score and using that feature's value as a context. It requires some changes in the training process which I'm not going to discuss right now. Here is an example of hard attention. ![show attend hard example]( 16: Hard attention visualization, white regions are the regions which model attends to, Source: [Show, Attend, and Tell: Neural Image Caption Generation with Visual Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03044) As you can see, the caption has changed. Now it's saying _"A man and a woman playing frisbee in a field."_ instead _"A woman is throwing a frisbee in a park."_. Attention regions are not fully related to the generated token (as in soft attention), when generating token `frisbee` model attends to the child. ## [lets abstract the attention permalink](https://erdem.pl/2021/05/introduction-to-attention-mechanism\#lets-abstract-the-attention) Let's abstract the Attention Now, when you know what the Attention is, we can start working on abstracting the idea to create the so-called _"Attention Layer"_. First, let's sum up what we have right now: - **Input vectors**: **X** (shape NXxDXN\_X \\times D\_XNX?xDX?) - **Query vector**: **q** (shape DQD\_QDQ?), this is our previous hidden state, but I've changed the color to purpule to match the work from "The Illustrated Transformer" - **Similarity function**: fattf\_{att}fatt? - **Similarities**: **e**, ei=fatt(q,Xi)e\_i = f\_{att}(\\textcolor{mediumpurple}{q}, \\textcolor{limegreen}{X\_i})ei?=fatt?(q,Xi?) - **Attention weights**: a=softmax(e)a = \\text{softmax}(e)a=softmax(e) (shape NXN\_XNX?) - **Output**: y=sumi(ai,Xi)y = \\sum\_i(a\_i,\\textcolor{limegreen}{X\_i})y=sumi?(ai?,Xi?) Currently, our similarity function is fattf\_{att}fatt? which was correct, base on early attention papers but for the generalization, we can change it to be a **dot product** between **q** and **X** vectors. This is just a lot more efficient to calculate dot product, but it creates one product with the end results. Training times are normalized relative to the standard Transformer at sequence length 512. The OOM results for standard Transformer occur during training when maintaining consistent batch sizes across all sequence lengths for fair comparison. With standard data parallelism, each GPU maintains a complete copy of the model, optimizer states, and gradients; thus, the 840GB = 320GB total memory cannot be pooled, and each GPU independently faces the 40GB memory constraint. The quadratic memory footprint includes: (1) the attention matrices (approximately 32GB per layer for batch size of 16 at 8192 tokens with mixed precision), (2) activation storage for backpropagation, (3) optimizer states (Adam requires 2 parameter memory), and (4) gradient accumulation. While it is possible to train longer sequences with reduced batch size or gradient checkpointing, we maintain consistent training configurations across all models for fair efficiency comparison. CPA demonstrates excellent scalability, with memory usage and computation time scaling linearly with sequence length. For short sequences (512 tokens), the efficiency gains are moderate compared to standard Transformers. However, as sequence length increases, the benefits become increasingly pronounced. At 8,192 tokens, standard Transformers run out of memory (OOM) on our hardware, while CPA continues to function efficiently. At 32,768 tokens, CPA maintains the lowest memory usage and highest inference speed among all compared models who went Out-Of-Memory. Figure 6 visualizes the scaling of memory usage with respect to sequence length, clearly showing the quadratic scaling of standard Transformers versus the linear scaling of CPA and other efficient attention variants. Ablation studies We conduct ablation studies to understand the contribution of different components in the CPA mechanism. Table 4 presents results on the WMT14 En-De translation task. Table 4. Ablation study results on WMT14 En-De translation. Model Variant BLEU Training time (hours) Peak memory (GB) CPA-Full 28.1 22.3 11.4 - Sparsemax (with Softmax) 27.9 22.5 12.3 - MLP (with Linear) 27.4 21.2 10.8 - Multi-head (Single-head) 26.8 20.5 10.3 - Learned GCV (with Mean) 27.6 21.8 10.9 Open in a new tab The top row shows our full CPA model. Subsequent rows show performance when removing or replacing each component. These results highlight the importance of each component: Using sparsemax instead of softmax provides a small but consistent performance improvement (+0.2 BLEU) The two-layer MLP for priority scoring is crucial for performance (+0.7 BLEU compared to linear) Multi-head attention remains important, as in standard Transformers (+1.3 BLEU versus single-head) The learned GCV provides meaningful gains over simple averaging (+0.5 BLEU) We also investigate how varying the sparsity level in our sparse attention allocation affects performance. Figure 7 shows performance on WMT14 En-De as a function of the number of tokens attended to (for the top-k variant). Fig. 7. Open in a new tab Performance (BLEU score) on WMT14 En-De as a function of sparsity level (percentage of tokens receiving non-zero attention). Performance improves rapidly as sparsity decreases from 1% to approximately 25%, then plateaus. This suggests that attending to a small subset of tokens is sufficient to capture most necessary information. Performance improves rapidly as k increases from 1% to approximately 25% of the sequence length, then plateaus, suggesting that attending to a small subset of tokens is sufficient to capture most of the necessary information. Analysis of learned attention patterns To better understand how CPA allocates attention, we visualize the sparse attention weights for different layers and heads on the WMT14 En-De translation task. Figure 8 shows attention visualizations for representative heads in different layers. Fig. 8. Open in a new tab Visualization of learned attention patterns in CPA. Each colored bar represents a token receiving non-zero attention, with color intensity indicating attention weight magnitude. (a-c) show patterns from different layers and heads, demonstrating increasing specialization from early to deeper layers. (d) shows average attention by position across all heads in the final layer. We observe several interesting patterns: Specialization by head: Different attention heads focus on different aspects of the input. Some heads attend primarily to content words (nouns, verbs), while others focus on function words or syntactic markers. Layer-specific behavior: Early layers (Figure 8a) tend to have more distributed attention, while deeper layers (Figure 8c) become increasingly focused on specific tokens that are semantically important for the current context. Context-dependent sparsity: The number of tokens receiving non-zero attention varies significantly based on the input complexity. Simple sentences result in very sparse attention (5-10% of tokens), while complex sentences with ambiguous references or specialized terminology lead to less sparse patterns (20-30% of tokens). Positional biases: Despite not explicitly encoding positional relationships in the attention mechanism, certain heads develop positional biases (Figure 8d), focusing on tokens near the beginning or end of the sequence. These observations suggest that CPA learns meaningful attention allocation strategies that adapt to input complexity, supporting our hypothesis that explicit pairwise comparisons are often redundant. Discussion Key findings Our experimental results demonstrate that Contextual Priority Attention achieves performance competitive with standard self-attention while significantly reducing computational costs. This supports our hypothesis that explicit pairwise token interactions may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. The global-to-local attention paradigm of CPA offers several advantages: Efficiency: Linear scaling with sequence length enables processing of much longer sequences than standard Transformers can handle. Our results show CPA can efficiently process sequences up to 32K tokens, where standard Transformers run out of memory. Interpretability: The sparse attention patterns highlight which tokens are most contextually relevant, providing insights into model decision-making. As shown in our analysis of attention patterns, CPA learns meaningful token prioritization strategies. Adaptivity: The number of tokens attended to naturally adapts to input complexity, allocating computational resources where needed. This results in more efficient processing of simple inputs while maintaining capacity for complex ones. Effectiveness on long sequences: CPA performs particularly well on long document tasks, where capturing both local and global context is essential. This makes it well-suited for applications like document-level machine translation, long-form question answering, and document summarization. Figure 9 illustrates the performance-complexity trade-off for different attention mechanisms. CPA achieves an attractive balance, delivering near-standard-Transformer performance with linear computational complexity. Fig. 9. Open in a new tab Performance vs. computational complexity for different attention mechanisms on the WMT14 En-De translation task. The ideal models would be in the top-left corner (high performance, low complexity). CPA achieves a favorable trade-off, approaching the performance of standard Transformers while maintaining linear complexity. Limitations Despite its promising results, CPA has several limitations that present opportunities for future research: Global context quality: The performance of CPA depends critically on the quality of the Global Context Vector. For very complex or ambiguous inputs, a single context vector may not capture all relevant aspects of the sequence. This limitation becomes more pronounced as sequence length increases beyond the sizes tested in our experiments. Task-specific performance: While CPA performs well across most tasks, it shows slightly lower performance on certain language modeling benchmarks. This suggests that some tasks may benefit more from exhaustive pairwise comparisons. Training dynamics: We observed that CPA models sometimes require more careful initialization and training compared to standard Transformers, likely due to the increased importance of the global context representation. Learning meaningful global representations early in training is crucial for model convergence. Theoretical capacity: While we prove that CPA can theoretically approximate standard attention, this approximation may require higher model capacity in practice. Our experiments compensated for this by slightly increasing the hidden dimensions in the priority scoring MLP. Hardware utilization: The sparse attention patterns in CPA, while theoretically efficient, may not fully utilize modern GPU hardware designed for dense matrix operations. Custom CUDA kernels for sparse operations help mitigate this issue but introduce additional implementation complexity. Future directions Our work opens several promising directions for future research: Hierarchical CPA: Creating hierarchical representations of global context at different granularities could help capture both fine-grained and high-level patterns. This approach would involve computing multiple context vectors at different levels of abstraction, from local windows to global document-level representations. Adaptive sparsity: Dynamically adjusting the sparsity level based on input complexity could further improve efficiency without sacrificing performance. This could be implemented by learning a threshold function that determines the minimum attention weight required for a token to be considered relevant. Causal CPA for auto-regressive generation: Our current implementation applies CPA only in encoder architectures. Extending CPA to efficient causal decoding in decoder-only models (like GPT-style architectures) requires careful design to handle incremental GCV updates. One promising approach is to maintain a running GCV that can be updated in time per generated token: . This would enable linear-time auto-regressive generation while maintaining the benefits of global context-driven attention. Cross-modal applications: The global context approach may be particularly well-suited for cross-modal attention, where different modalities (text, image, audio) require different attention patterns. For example, in multimodal tasks, separate global context vectors could be computed for each modality, then used to guide cross-modal attention. Theoretical exploration: Further theoretical analysis of the expressivity-efficiency tradeoff in different attention mechanisms could guide the development of even more efficient variants. This includes a deeper understanding of what types of dependencies can be captured by global-context-based attention versus explicit pairwise attention. Pre-training and transfer learning: Investigating how CPA performs in large-scale pre-training scenarios and subsequent fine-tuning could reveal its potential for more efficient foundation models. The linear scaling properties of CPA make it particularly promising for very large models trained on extensive datasets. Hardware optimization: CPA's sparse attention patterns could enable specialized hardware implementations for even greater efficiency gains. Future research could explore hardware designs specifically optimized for global-context-based sparse attention mechanisms. We believe the hierarchical CPA and adaptive sparsity approaches represent the most immediate opportunities for significant improvements. Fig. 10. Conclusion We presented Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), a novel attention mechanism that achieves theoretical complexity while empirically demonstrating linear scaling and maintaining competitive performance with standard Transformers. By reimagining attention as a global-context-driven priority system rather than exhaustive pairwise comparisons, CPA offers significant efficiency improvements, particularly for long sequences. Our experimental results across diverse tasks demonstrate that CPA achieves performance comparable to full attention while scaling more efficiently to long inputs. The emergent attention patterns reveal that CPA learns meaningful prioritization strategies that adapt to input complexity. On the Long Range Arena benchmark specifically designed to test long-range modeling capabilities, CPA outperforms other efficient attention variants by a significant margin. The success of CPA suggests that the quadratic computational complexity of standard self-attention may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. By focusing computational resources on the most contextually relevant tokens, CPA provides an efficient alternative that scales better to the increasingly long contexts required by modern NLP applications. The ability to process sequences of tens of thousands of tokens efficiently opens up new possibilities for applications such as document-level translation, long-form question answering, and full-document summarization. DEEP LEARNING Unpacking the Power of Attention Mechanisms in Deep Learning Attention mechanisms enable models to focus on specific parts of input data, enhancing their ability to process sequences effectively. GAUDENZ BOESCH ? MAR 26, 2024 ? 10 MIN READ Attention mechanisms allow artificial intelligence (AI) models to dynamically focus on individual elements within visual data. This mimics the way humans concentrate on specific visual elements at a time. This enhances the interpretability of AI systems for applications in computer vision and natural language processing (NLP). The introduction of the Transformer model was a significant leap forward for the concept of attention in deep learning. Vaswani et al. described this model in the seminal paper titled "Attention is All You Need" in 2017. Uniquely, this model did not rely on conventional neural network architectures like convolutional or recurrent layers. without conventional neural networks. This represented a significant departure in how machine learning models process sequential data. Addressing Data Processing Attention mechanisms address a critical challenge in AI: the efficient processing of vast and complex data sets. By enabling models to selectively weigh the importance of different input features, they improve both accuracy and efficiency. This makes these models perform better for tasks such as image recognition, text translation, and speech recognition. For instance, in computer vision, models with attention mechanisms can better understand scenes by focusing on relevant objects. This has positive implications for applications like autonomous vehicles and facial recognition systems. Furthermore, attention mechanisms work to enhance the explainability or interpretability of AI models. This involves developing insights into which parts of the data the model considers most important. In a way, you can consider it offering a window into the "thought processes" of AI.
