Linear Attention as In-Context Learners Beyond the efficiency gains offered by linear attention mechanisms, a significant advancement lies in their application to enhancein-context learning. This refers to the capability of a model to rapidly adapt or learn from a given prompt without requiring explicit gradient updates to its pre-trained weights. While large Transformer models inherently exhibit in-context learning by interpreting the prompt as a form of training data, recent innovations have integrated fast learning rules directly into the attention mechanism, effectively treating sequence processing as an online training process.FWP[ 50] establish a formal equivalence between existing linear attention mechanisms and fast weight learning. In the FWP paradigm, a slow neural network learns to program the "fast weights" of another network, often via additive outer products of self-invented key and value patterns. This section explores several models, including DeltaNet [71, 72], Longhorn [30], Test-Time Training (TTT) layers [51, 52], Titans [3], that exemplify this paradigm of leveraging linear attention as an in-context learner through mechanisms like fast weight updates, viewed through a meta-learning lens. Training times are normalized relative to the standard Transformer at sequence length 512. The OOM results for standard Transformer occur during training when maintaining consistent batch sizes across all sequence lengths for fair comparison. With standard data parallelism, each GPU maintains a complete copy of the model, optimizer states, and gradients; thus, the 840GB = 320GB total memory cannot be pooled, and each GPU independently faces the 40GB memory constraint. The quadratic memory footprint includes: (1) the attention matrices (approximately 32GB per layer for batch size of 16 at 8192 tokens with mixed precision), (2) activation storage for backpropagation, (3) optimizer states (Adam requires 2 parameter memory), and (4) gradient accumulation. While it is possible to train longer sequences with reduced batch size or gradient checkpointing, we maintain consistent training configurations across all models for fair efficiency comparison. CPA demonstrates excellent scalability, with memory usage and computation time scaling linearly with sequence length. For short sequences (512 tokens), the efficiency gains are moderate compared to standard Transformers. However, as sequence length increases, the benefits become increasingly pronounced. At 8,192 tokens, standard Transformers run out of memory (OOM) on our hardware, while CPA continues to function efficiently. At 32,768 tokens, CPA maintains the lowest memory usage and highest inference speed among all compared models who went Out-Of-Memory. Figure 6 visualizes the scaling of memory usage with respect to sequence length, clearly showing the quadratic scaling of standard Transformers versus the linear scaling of CPA and other efficient attention variants. Subsequent rows show performance when removing or replacing each component. These results highlight the importance of each component: Using sparsemax instead of softmax provides a small but consistent performance improvement (+0.2 BLEU) The two-layer MLP for priority scoring is crucial for performance (+0.7 BLEU compared to linear) Multi-head attention remains important, as in standard Transformers (+1.3 BLEU versus single-head) The learned GCV provides meaningful gains over simple averaging (+0.5 BLEU) We also investigate how varying the sparsity level in our sparse attention allocation affects performance. Figure 7 shows performance on WMT14 En-De as a function of the number of tokens attended to (for the top-k variant). Fig. 7. Open in a new tab Performance (BLEU score) on WMT14 En-De as a function of sparsity level (percentage of tokens receiving non-zero attention). Performance improves rapidly as sparsity decreases from 1% to approximately 25%, then plateaus. This suggests that attending to a small subset of tokens is sufficient to capture most necessary information. Performance improves rapidly as k increases from 1% to approximately 25% of the sequence length, then plateaus, suggesting that attending to a small subset of tokens is sufficient to capture most of the necessary information. Analysis of learned attention patterns To better understand how CPA allocates attention, we visualize the sparse attention weights for different layers and heads on the WMT14 En-De translation task. Figure 8 shows attention visualizations for representative heads in different layers. Fig. 8. Open in a new tab Visualization of learned attention patterns in CPA. Each colored bar represents a token receiving non-zero attention, with color intensity indicating attention weight magnitude. (a-c) show patterns from different layers and heads, demonstrating increasing specialization from early to deeper layers. (d) shows average attention by position across all heads in the final layer. We observe several interesting patterns: Specialization by head: Different attention heads focus on different aspects of the input. Some heads attend primarily to content words (nouns, verbs), while others focus on function words or syntactic markers. Layer-specific behavior: Early layers (Figure 8a) tend to have more distributed attention, while deeper layers (Figure 8c) become increasingly focused on specific tokens that are semantically important for the current context. Context-dependent sparsity: The number of tokens receiving non-zero attention varies significantly based on the input complexity. Simple sentences result in very sparse attention (5-10% of tokens), while complex sentences with ambiguous references or specialized terminology lead to less sparse patterns (20-30% of tokens). Positional biases: Despite not explicitly encoding positional relationships in the attention mechanism, certain heads develop positional biases (Figure 8d), focusing on tokens near the beginning or end of the sequence. These observations suggest that CPA learns meaningful attention allocation strategies that adapt to input complexity, supporting our hypothesis that explicit pairwise comparisons are often redundant. Discussion Key findings Our experimental results demonstrate that Contextual Priority Attention achieves performance competitive with standard self-attention while significantly reducing computational costs. This supports our hypothesis that explicit pairwise token interactions may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. The global-to-local attention paradigm of CPA offers several advantages: Efficiency: Linear scaling with sequence length enables processing of much longer sequences than standard Transformers can handle. Our results show CPA can efficiently process sequences up to 32K tokens, where standard Transformers run out of memory. Interpretability: The sparse attention patterns highlight which tokens are most contextually relevant, providing insights into model decision-making. As shown in our analysis of attention patterns, CPA learns meaningful token prioritization strategies. Adaptivity: The number of tokens attended to naturally adapts to input complexity, allocating computational resources where needed. This results in more efficient processing of simple inputs while maintaining capacity for complex ones. Effectiveness on long sequences: CPA performs particularly well on long document tasks, where capturing both local and global context is essential. This makes it well-suited for applications like document-level machine translation, long-form question answering, and document summarization. Figure 9 illustrates the performance-complexity trade-off for different attention mechanisms. CPA achieves an attractive balance, delivering near-standard-Transformer performance with linear computational complexity. Fig. 9. Open in a new tab Performance vs. computational complexity for different attention mechanisms on the WMT14 En-De translation task. The ideal models would be in the top-left corner (high performance, low complexity). CPA achieves a favorable trade-off, approaching the performance of standard Transformers while maintaining linear complexity. Limitations Despite its promising results, CPA has several limitations that present opportunities for future research: Global context quality: The performance of CPA depends critically on the quality of the Global Context Vector. For very complex or ambiguous inputs, a single context vector may not capture all relevant aspects of the sequence. This limitation becomes more pronounced as sequence length increases beyond the sizes tested in our experiments. Task-specific performance: While CPA performs well across most tasks, it shows slightly lower performance on certain language modeling benchmarks. This suggests that some tasks may benefit more from exhaustive pairwise comparisons. Training dynamics: We observed that CPA models sometimes require more careful initialization and training compared to standard Transformers, likely due to the increased importance of the global context representation. Learning meaningful global representations early in training is crucial for model convergence. Theoretical capacity: While we prove that CPA can theoretically approximate standard attention, this approximation may require higher model capacity in practice. Our experiments compensated for this by slightly increasing the hidden dimensions in the priority scoring MLP. Hardware utilization: The sparse attention patterns in CPA, while theoretically efficient, may not fully utilize modern GPU hardware designed for dense matrix operations. Custom CUDA kernels for sparse operations help mitigate this issue but introduce additional implementation complexity. Future directions Our work opens several promising directions for future research: Hierarchical CPA: Creating hierarchical representations of global context at different granularities could help capture both fine-grained and high-level patterns. This approach would involve computing multiple context vectors at different levels of abstraction, from local windows to global document-level representations. Adaptive sparsity: Dynamically adjusting the sparsity level based on input complexity could further improve efficiency without sacrificing performance. This could be implemented by learning a threshold function that determines the minimum attention weight required for a token to be considered relevant. Causal CPA for auto-regressive generation: Our current implementation applies CPA only in encoder architectures. Extending CPA to efficient causal decoding in decoder-only models (like GPT-style architectures) requires careful design to handle incremental GCV updates. One promising approach is to maintain a running GCV that can be updated in time per generated token: . This would enable linear-time auto-regressive generation while maintaining the benefits of global context-driven attention. Cross-modal applications: The global context approach may be particularly well-suited for cross-modal attention, where different modalities (text, image, audio) require different attention patterns. For example, in multimodal tasks, separate global context vectors could be computed for each modality, then used to guide cross-modal attention. Theoretical exploration: Further theoretical analysis of the expressivity-efficiency tradeoff in different attention mechanisms could guide the development of even more efficient variants. This includes a deeper understanding of what types of dependencies can be captured by global-context-based attention versus explicit pairwise attention. Pre-training and transfer learning: Investigating how CPA performs in large-scale pre-training scenarios and subsequent fine-tuning could reveal its potential for more efficient foundation models. The linear scaling properties of CPA make it particularly promising for very large models trained on extensive datasets. Hardware optimization: CPA's sparse attention patterns could enable specialized hardware implementations for even greater efficiency gains. Future research could explore hardware designs specifically optimized for global-context-based sparse attention mechanisms. Figure 10 illustrates these potential future directions, highlighting their relative complexity and potential impact. We believe the hierarchical CPA and adaptive sparsity approaches represent the most immediate opportunities for significant improvements. Fig. 10. Open in a new tab Potential future directions for extending Contextual Priority Attention. Each path represents a promising avenue for research, with estimated complexity and potential impact. Conclusion We presented Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), a novel attention mechanism that achieves theoretical complexity while empirically demonstrating linear scaling and maintaining competitive performance with standard Transformers. By reimagining attention as a global-context-driven priority system rather than exhaustive pairwise comparisons, CPA offers significant efficiency improvements, particularly for long sequences. Our experimental results across diverse tasks demonstrate that CPA achieves performance comparable to full attention while scaling more efficiently to long inputs. The emergent attention patterns reveal that CPA learns meaningful prioritization strategies that adapt to input complexity. On the Long Range Arena benchmark specifically designed to test long-range modeling capabilities, CPA outperforms other efficient attention variants by a significant margin. The success of CPA suggests that the quadratic computational complexity of standard self-attention may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. By focusing computational resources on the most contextually relevant tokens, CPA provides an efficient alternative that scales better to the increasingly long contexts required by modern NLP applications. The ability to process sequences of tens of thousands of tokens efficiently opens up new possibilities for applications such as document-level translation, long-form question answering, and full-document summarization. Learn more: PMC Disclaimer | PMC Copyright Notice Sci Rep. 2025 Dec 17;16:2869. doi: 10.1038/s41598-025-32639-x Contextual priority attention enables linear time sequence modeling in transformers Karim Ben Khaled 1,2,?, Davy Monticolo 1,2 Author information Article notes Copyright and License information PMCID: PMC12828051 PMID: 41408385 Abstract The quadratic computational complexity of the self-attention mechanism in Transformer models severely constrains their applicability to long sequence inputs. We propose Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), a novel attention mechanism that reduces computational complexity from to theoretically, with experimentally observed linear scaling, while preserving the essential contextual modeling capabilities of traditional attention. Unlike existing efficient attention variants that approximate the full attention matrix, CPA fundamentally reimagines attention as a global-context-driven priority system. Our approach first computes a Global Context Vector (GCV) to capture the overall sequence information, then uses this context to assign priority scores to individual tokens, enabling sparse attention allocation. In encoder-decoder architectures, we apply CPA to the encoder while maintaining standard attention in the decoder, achieving substantial efficiency improvements while preserving full model expressivity for sequence-to-sequence tasks. Through theoretical analysis and extensive experimentation across language understanding, translation, and long document tasks, we demonstrate that CPA achieves comparable performance to standard self-attention while offering significant efficiency gains. On long-sequence benchmarks (8K+ tokens), CPA outperforms traditional Transformers and state-of-the-art efficient attention variants while using substantially fewer computational resources. Our findings suggest that pairwise token interactions may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling, opening new avenues for efficient large-scale language models. Subject terms: Engineering, Mathematics and computing Introduction Transformer-based models1 have revolutionized natural language processing and many other domains of artificial intelligence. Their success stems largely from the self-attention mechanism, which enables each element in a sequence to attend to all other elements, capturing complex dependencies regardless of positional distance. However, this attention mechanism scales quadratically with sequence length, leading to significant computational and memory constraints when processing long inputs. This quadratic scaling poses a fundamental challenge for applications requiring long context, such as document-level machine translation, long-form question answering, and whole-document analysis. While various approaches have been proposed to address this bottleneck2-5, most attempt to approximate standard self-attention through techniques such as low-rank approximations, localized attention patterns, or kernel methods. In this paper, we introduce Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), which takes a fundamentally different approach. Rather than approximating the pairwise attention matrix, CPA reimagines attention as a global-to-local relevance filtering process inspired by cognitive theories of human attention6,7. Our approach first computes a Global Context Vector (GCV) that captures the "big picture" of the input sequence. Then, using this global context, we compute a priority score for each input element, measuring its relevance to the current context. Finally, we apply a sparse transformation to these scores, allowing the model to focus exclusively on the most relevant elements (see Fig. 1). Fig. 1. Open in a new tab Overview of the Contextual Priority Attention mechanism. (a) First, a Global Context Vector (GCV) is computed from the input sequence using a learned weighted average. (b) The GCV is concatenated with each token to compute token-specific priority scores via an MLP. (c) Sparse attention weights are generated by applying sparsemax to the priority scores. (d) The output is computed as a weighted sum of value projections, using only tokens with non-zero attention weights. CPA offers several key advantages: Linear computational complexity () with respect to sequence length Interpretable attention patterns with explicit token prioritization Adaptive sparsity that adjusts to input complexity Theoretical capacity to capture both local and global dependencies Through extensive experimentation on multiple tasks including machine translation, language modeling, and long document classification, we demonstrate that CPA achieves performance competitive with full attention while significantly reducing computational requirements, especially for long sequences. Our contributions are as follows: We propose Contextual Priority Attention, a novel attention mechanism with theoretical complexity that empirically demonstrates linear scaling, based on global-context-driven prioritization. We provide theoretical analysis showing that CPA can approximate full attention under certain conditions while maintaining linear complexity. We empirically demonstrate competitive performance with state-of-the-art models across multiple tasks. We analyze the emergent attention patterns, showing how CPA learns meaningful prioritization strategies. Related work Efficient attention mechanisms The quadratic complexity of self-attention has inspired numerous approaches to improve efficiency. These can be broadly categorized into several strategies: Pattern-based sparsity: Methods like Sparse Transformer2 and Longformer8 limit attention to predefined patterns, such as local windows, dilated windows, or fixed global tokens. BlockBERT9 and BigBird10 use block-sparse attention patterns. While effective, these approaches incorporate structural biases that may not align with the actual dependencies in the data. Learnable sparsity: Methods such as Reformer3 use locality-sensitive hashing to dynamically identify similar tokens that should attend to each other. Routing Transformer11 employs content-based clustering. These approaches reduce complexity but still fundamentally rely on pairwise token interactions. Low-rank approximations: Linformer4 projects the key and value matrices to lower dimensions, achieving linear complexity. However, this approach struggles with variable-length inputs and loses the flexibility of the original attention mechanism. Kernel methods: Performers5 and Linear Transformers12 rewrite the softmax attention using kernel methods, approximating the attention matrix implicitly. While mathematically elegant, these methods may sacrifice some of the expressivity of the original attention mechanism. Recurrence-based methods: Models like Transformer-XL13 and Compressive Transformer14 incorporate recurrence to handle long sequences. These approaches maintain the standard attention within segments but use recurrent connections between segments. Table 1 provides a comparative analysis of these approaches. Our Contextual Priority Attention differs fundamentally from these approaches by eliminating pairwise comparisons entirely, instead using global context to guide token-specific attention allocation. Table 1. Comparison of efficient attention approaches. Approach Complexity Preserves full expressivity Handles variable length inputs Learnable patterns Implementation complexity Standard attention Low Pattern-based Sparsity Medium Learnable Sparsity Partial High Low-Rank Approximations Partial Medium Kernel Methods Partial Partial Medium Recurrence-based + Memory Partial High CPA (Ours) Theoretical Medium Open in a new tab Cognitive models of attention Our approach is loosely inspired by cognitive theories of human attention, which suggest that perception involves both bottom-up feature processing and top-down attentional control guided by current goals and context15,16. Particularly relevant is Broadbent's filter theory7, which proposes that cognitive processing employs selective filters to focus only on relevant stimuli. In neuroscience, the interaction between global brain states and local neural activity parallels our approach of using global context to guide local attention allocation17. Several computational models of attention in computer vision have implemented related concepts, particularly through top-down modulation of bottom-up saliency18,19. Sparse neural networks Our work also relates to research on sparse neural networks, particularly approaches that dynamically determine sparsity patterns. Techniques such as Sparse Mixture of Experts20,21 and conditional computation22,23 activate only relevant parts of the network based on input. These approaches demonstrate that sparse activation can achieve strong performance while improving computational efficiency. Contextual priority attention In this section, we describe our proposed Contextual Priority Attention mechanism in detail, first presenting the intuition and then formalizing the approach. Intuition Traditional self-attention computes pairwise interactions between all tokens in a sequence, requiring comparisons for a sequence of length n. This exhaustive approach implicitly assumes that every token-to-token relationship is potentially informative and must be explicitly evaluated. However, this assumption may be unnecessarily conservative for many natural language tasks, where the semantic content of a sequence can often be summarized more compactly. Human attention operates fundamentally differently. Cognitive research suggests that we do not exhaustively compare every perceived element to every other element. Instead, we rapidly construct a holistic understanding of our environment-a "gist" or mental model-and then selectively attend to elements that are most relevant to our current goals and context16,24. This two-stage process of global comprehension followed by selective focus allows humans to efficiently process complex scenes without cognitive overload. CPA draws direct inspiration from this cognitive model. Rather than asking "how relevant is token A to token B?" for all possible pairs, we decompose attention into two sequential stages: Global comprehension: First, we compute a Global Context Vector (GCV) that captures a compressed, holistic representation of the entire input sequence. This vector serves as a summary of "what is this sequence about?" Selective prioritization: Then, for each token, we evaluate a single question: "how relevant is this token to the global context?" This yields a priority score indicating contextual importance. This reformulation reduces the computational burden from pairwise comparisons to n context-relative evaluations, while preserving the essential selective nature of attention. Figure 2 illustrates this fundamental conceptual difference between standard self-attention and CPA. Fig. 2. Open in a new tab Conceptual comparison between standard self-attention (left) and Contextual Priority Attention (right). Standard attention computes all pairwise interactions between tokens, resulting in quadratic complexity. CPA first computes a global context representation, then evaluates each token against this shared context, achieving linear complexity. To illustrate with a concrete example, consider processing the sentence: "The cat, which had been sleeping peacefully on the warm windowsill all afternoon, suddenly jumped down." Standard self-attention would compute interactions, including many between tokens with minimal semantic relationship (e.g., "peacefully" and "down"). In contrast, CPA first forms a global understanding that this sentence describes a cat's action, then prioritizes tokens most relevant to this context-likely "cat," "sleeping," and "jumped"-while assigning lower priority to modifiers and function words. This approach offers an additional benefit beyond computational efficiency: it provides an implicit regularization effect. By forcing the model to route all attention decisions through a shared global context, CPA encourages the learning of representations that capture semantically meaningful aspects of the input rather than spurious local correlations. The global context acts as an information bottleneck25, filtering out noise while retaining task-relevant signal. By computing relevance scores against a shared global context, we can prioritize tokens holistically, focusing computational resources on the most contextually important elements while naturally filtering out irrelevant ones. This design philosophy "global understanding before local selection" mirrors not only human cognition but also efficient algorithms in other domains, such as hierarchical search and coarse-to-fine processing in computer vision26. Architecture of different stacked models. 4. Pretrained LLM with Efficient Attention 4.1. Pretrained Models with Uniform Efficient Attention While early explorations of linear attention were often confined to smaller-scale models, recent advancements have demonstrated their successful scalability to the multi-billion parameter range, establishing them as viable and highly efficient alternatives to the standard Transformer. These models, built purely on linear attention or its architectural equivalents like State-Space Models (SSMs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), retain their signature inference effi- ciency even at large scales. RWKV-based modelThe RWKV project represents a sustained and influential effort to create a scalable Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) architecture that combines the parallelizable training of Transformers with the efficient inference of traditional RNNs [38]. For instance, the EAGLE (RWKV-5) series introduced matrix-valued states to increase capacity, while subsequent iterations like Finch (RWKV-6) [39] and Goose (RWKV-7) [40] incorporated dynamic recurrence and expressive state evolution mechanisms (e.g., a delta-rule) to enable more complex, data- dependent state transitions. Mamba-based modelThe success of the Mamba architecture [ 17], with its data-dependent selection mechanism (Section 2.2.2), has spurred a wave of adoption and scaling initiatives from major research labs.Falcon Mamba[ 79] is based on the pure Mamba-based architecture to demonstrate performance competitive with leading Transformer models on a wide range of general-purpose language benchmarks, validating the architecture's viability for such tasks while retaining its signature constant-time inference. Further evidence of this paradigm's potential is provided byCodestral Mamba[ 36], built on the Mamba-2 architecture. While specialized for code generation, it achieves state-of-the-art results on relevant benchmarks and supports a 256k token context, demonstrating the scalability and effectiveness of the SSM approach within a complex and structured domain. Sparse-based modelMiniCPM-4 [ 58] introduces a two-stage sparse attention mechanism that dynamically selects relevant key-value blocks for each query token based on semantic similarity. MiniCPM-4 leverages InfLLM-v2, a Block Sparse Attention variant to replace standard 18 Attention mechanism. Moreover, a lightweight LogSumExp approximation enables efficient top- k selection, making the method scalable to extremely long sequences. Together, these techniques allow MiniCPM-4 to balance fine-grained contextual awareness with tractable memory and compute requirements, making it a strong candidate for long-context modeling. 4.2. Pretrained Models with Hybrid Efficient Attention With the increasing demand for efficient long-context modeling and diverse computational paradigms, recent research has extensively explored hybrid attention mechanisms. Such strate- gies combine global and local attention components, often interleaving specialized layers to balance computational cost and performance. The candidate model architecture illustrations are shown in Figure 4. Sparse Hybrid ModelGPT-3 [ 5] integrates a hybrid attention mechanism by interleaving dense and locally banded sparse attention layers, inspired by the Sparse Transformer [8]. Dense attention provides full-context modeling, while sparse layers adopt fixed or strided patterns to reduce the number of attended tokens. This design enables GPT-3 to efficiently scale to large model sizes using a fixed context window of 2048 tokens, balancing modeling capacity and computational efficiency. Linear-Full Hybrid ModelJamba [ 28] and MiniMax-01 [26] combine linear and full attention layers to achieve an efficient trade-off between throughput and expressiveness. MiniMax-01 employs Lightning Attention across most layers, inserting Softmax-based full attention every eight layers. Jamba adopts a similar ratio, inserting one Transformer layer into every eight-layer Mamba block. Both achieve faster decoding and improved long-sequence performance by limiting the use of computationally intensive full attention. Local-Full Hybrid ModelGemma 3 [ 57], Command A [ 67], and LLaMA-4-Maverick [ 33] alternate between local and global attention layers, with a shared design philosophy of using global layers sparsely, e.g., every 4-6 layers, to enhance efficiency. While local layers adopt sliding-window patterns, the key difference lies in position encoding strategies. Gemma 3 modulates RoPE base frequencies-assigning 10K for local and 1M for global layers-to better capture long-range dependencies. Command A and LLaMA-4-Maverick mixes RoPE-based local layers with full attention layers that omit positional embeddings entirely, allowing stronger long sequence performance. Advanced Hybrid ModelCharacter.AI [ 6] interleaves local attention with sliding windows and sparse global attention layers applied every six layers. Especially, they resue global attention layer's key-value representations across multiple non-adjacent layers. This KV sharing mecha- nism enables efficient long-context processing with reduced memory and latency overhead. YOCO [54] and Phi-4-mini-flash [48] adopt a dual-decoder architecture that separates the prefill and generation phases. The Self-Decoder utilizes linear attention mechanisms such as RetNet and Sliding-Window Attention for both prefill and generation, while the Cross-Decoder is activated only during generation. A single-layer global KV cache is used throughout, allowing linear-time prefill and efficient decoding with minimal GPU memory consumption. 19 In summary, these recent advances underscore the trend toward hybridizing attention mechanisms to achieve balanced performance across varying computational constraints and sequence lengths. Each architecture uniquely contributes insights into effectively combining local detail management with global context integration, thereby providing valuable frameworks for future attention mechanism developments. 5. TAKEAWAYS Based on the current trajectory of both academic research and industrial deployment, several key consensus points emerge regarding the design of efficient attention mechanisms. The Superiority of HybridityThere is a growing consensus that while purely linear attention architectures offer impressive inference speeds, they frequently incur a non-trivial performance penalty in complex reasoning and ultra-long context retrieval. Consequently, hybrid models have emerged as the preferred architecture. These designs not only maintain the near-lossless performance of standard Transformers but demonstrate the potential to exceed them by balanc- ing global associative memory with precise local retrieval. School of Mathematical Sciences University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Editor: My editor Abstract Attention mechanism has been extensively integrated within mainstream neural network architectures, such as Transformers and graph attention networks. Yet, its underlying working principles remain somewhat elusive. What is its essence? Are there any connec- tions between it and traditional machine learning algorithms? In this study, we inspect the process of computing similarity using classic metrics and vector space properties in manifold learning, clustering, and supervised learning. We identify the key characteristics of similarity computation and information propagation in these methods and demonstrate that the self-attention mechanism in deep learning adheres to the same principles but op- erates more flexibly and adaptively. We decompose the self-attention mechanism into a learnable pseudo-metric function and an information propagation process based on similar- ity computation. We prove that the self-attention mechanism converges to a drift-diffusion process through continuous modeling provided the pseudo-metric is a transformation of a metric and certain reasonable assumptions hold. This equation could be transformed into a heat equation under a new metric. In addition, we give a first-order analysis of attention mechanism with a general pseudo-metric function. This study aids in understanding the effects and principle of attention mechanism through physical intuition. Finally, we pro- pose a modified attention mechanism called metric-attention by leveraging the concept of metric learning to facilitate the ability to learn desired metrics more effectively. Experi- mental results demonstrate that it outperforms self-attention regarding training efficiency, accuracy, and robustness. Keywords Attention mechanism, Transformer, graph attention network, similarity computation, heat diffusion 1 Introduction The attention or self-attention mechanism is extensively applied in popular deep learning architectures like Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2018) and graph attention networks (Veli? ckovi´ c et al., 2017). This mechanism enables the model to assign diverse ©2024 Tianyu Ruan and Shihua Zhang. License: CC-BY 4.0, seehttps://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Attribution requirements are provided at http://jmlr.org/papers/v23/21-0000.html. arXiv:2412.18288v1 [cs.LG] 24 Dec 2024 Tianyu Ruan and Shihua Zhang weights to various parts (data points, nodes, etc.) of the input sequence (data, graph, etc.) based on their relevance when producing an output. This capability is particularly critical for handling inputs where the lengths and relevance strengths of different parts can vary significantly. As a result, this mechanism contributes to the broad applications of deep learning in various fields, including natural language processing (Devlin et al., 2018; Brown et al., 2020; Radford et al., 2019), computer vision (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2021; Carion et al., 2020), graph mining (Liu et al., 2023) and bioinformatics (Dong and Zhang, 2022; Zhang et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2021). However, understanding the mathematical principle of attention mechanism is still chal- lenging due to its interaction with normalization layers and feed-forward networks in neural network architectures. Difficulties in understanding attention mechanism also stem from the numerous parameters in neural networks and various engineering techniques. To our knowledge, only a few studies have explored it in depth (Vuckovic et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2021; Sander et al., 2022; Geshkovski et al., 2023). Sander et al. (2022) formalized the self-attention mechanism with residual connections as a flow map and analyzed it from the perspective of the Wasserstein gradient flow. In addition, they characterized the L2 self- attention (Kim et al., 2021) using continuous dynamical systems. Geshkovski et al. (2023) investigated attention mechanism in Transformers by assuming that data is distributed on the unit sphere and making simplified assumptions about parameters and proved that the distribution would converge to a single point under certain conditions, suggesting that at- tention mechanism induces an aggregation tendency. However, they did not fully explain how attention mechanism works or its connection to classical algorithms. Moreover, several architectures, such as CRATE (Yu et al., 2024) and Probabilistic Transformer (Wu and Tu, 2023), have been proposed. They often originate from inter- pretable models and have information propagation mechanisms similar to attention mecha- nism. While not strictly equivalent, they offer valuable insights into understanding attention mechanism. For example, CRATE suggests that attention mechanism functions as a com- pression process, whereas the Probabilistic Transformer explains it as an explicit iteration of the Frank-Wolfe optimization algorithm. We illustrate three architecture components, i.e., the residual block, the attention block, and their recombination of a Transformer block (Figure 1). The attention block consists of an information propagation process followed by a linear transformation. Some studies modeled the residual block using an ordinary differential equation (E, 2017; Chen et al., 2018). Some researchers modeled the recombination of the residual and attention blocks using the flow map mentioned above. In this paper, we focus on the attention-based in- formation propagation mechanism. This mechanism can be viewed as a message-passing process akin to that in graph neural networks (GNNs) operating on fully connected graphs. However, GNNs typically employ fixed edge weights and topologies, which limit theoretical analysis to diffusion processes on graphs (Li et al., 2024). In contrast, attention mechanism, as a learnable method of information propagation on fully connected graphs, has yet to be thoroughly analyzed in terms of its limit behavior. Many machine learning methods such as manifold learning (e.g., diffusion map (Coif- man and Lafon, 2006), UMAP (McInnes et al., 2018)), clustering methods (e.g., k-means clustering (Lloyd, 1982), fuzzy c-means clustering (Bezdek et al., 1984), Markov cluster- ing (Van Dongen, 2008)) and supervised learning (e.g., k-nearest neighbors algorithm (Fix, 2 Towards Understanding how attention mechanism works in deep learning 1985), support vector machine (Cortes and Vapnik, 1995)), involve computing similarity or dissimilarity for pairwise data points (or nodes in a graph). These approaches usually consist of some of the following components successively: (1) Initializing similarity based on the input data and the adopted pseudo-metric; (2) Strengthening similarity through some transformation to make similar data points more similar or dissimilar ones more distinct; (3) Normalizing similarity to transform the similarity matrix into a type of probability distribution, which allows the use of probabilistic tools for comparison or further manipu- lation. Traditional algorithms aim to compute similarity by combining classic metrics and handcrafted designs to capture data features or extract information. Figure 1: Illustration of three ar- chitecture components in- cluding the residual block (A), the attention block (C), and their recombina- tion (B) of a Transformer block. We can intuitively observe that attention mech- anism also follows this principle of similarity com- putation to capture the inherent patterns in data. In this study, by exploring the common approach of similarity computation in classic machine learn- ing algorithms, we explain how this technique is uti- lized in attention mechanism, thereby revealing its connections to classical machine learning algorithms. In addition, we illustrate that under certain assump- tions like (1) the formulation of similarity can be de- composed into a transformation of a learnable met- ric function, a parameter on time scale and a soft- max similarity computation; (2) the time-scale pa- rameter is sufficiently small and (3) the manifold hy- pothesis holds, and there are sufficient data points sampled i.i.d. from a continuous distribution, at- tention mechanism for information propagation can be approximated by a drift-diffusion process on the manifold. Furthermore, we prove that, under certain assumptions, this process can be reformalized as a heat diffusion process under a new metric. This pro- vides theoretical support for intuitively understand- ing the working principle of the self-attention mech- anism through physical intuition (Figure 2). In assumption (1), if the learnable function is a general function rather than a metric function, we can still give a first-order analysis to describe the information propagation process of attention mecha- nism. Although this process does not generally cor- respond to a continuous dynamical system, it retains a similar interpretation to the metric version. That is to say, the zeroth-order effect is determined by the nearest data points, while the first- order effect relates to a drift-diffusion process at these points. The main difference between the two lies in how the nearest data points are defined. From the perspective of similarity computation, we decompose the self-attention mecha- nism into an information propagation process based on handcrafted similarity computation 3 Tianyu Ruan and Shihua Zhang and a learnable pseudo-metric. Inspired by this, we propose a modified attention mechanism by leveraging the concept of metric learning to enhance the ability to learn desired metrics more effectively. We refer to this modified attention mechanism as 'metric-attention'. Figure 2: Illustration of the main idea. (a) Attention mechanism consists of two main steps: (1) computing the similarity between nodes (data points or tokens), followed by propagating node features to neighboring nodes, weighted by the similarities, and (2) updating the features of the nodes. (b) Illustration of a drift-diffusion process on the manifold where data reside. This process is driven by two main forces: density guidance, which encourages local concentration, and diffusion, which promotes global consistency of features. We also introduce a first-order analysis of information propagation in a generalized pseudo-metric setting. Tsinghua University Abstract Transformer-based architectures have become the prevailing backbone of large language models. However, the quadratic time and memory complexity of self-attention remains a fundamental obstacle to efficient long-context modeling. To address this limitation, recent research has introduced two principal categories of efficient attention mechanisms. Linear attention methods achieve linear complexity through kernel approximations, recurrent formulations, or fast- weight dynamics, thereby enabling scalable inference with reduced computational overhead. Sparse attention techniques, in contrast, limit attention computation to selected subsets of tokens based on fixed patterns, block-wise routing, or clustering strategies, enhancing efficiency while preserving contextual coverage. This survey provides a systematic and comprehensive overview of these developments, integrating both algorithmic innovations and hardware-level considerations. In addition, we analyze the incorporation of efficient attention into large- scale pre-trained language models, including both architectures built entirely on efficient attention and hybrid designs that combine local and global components. By aligning theoretical foundations with practical deployment strategies, this work aims to serve as a foundational reference for advancing the design of scalable and efficient language models. Introduction Transformer-based architectures [61] have become the de-facto choice as the backbone of modern Large Language Models (LLMs). Despite their success, the standard self-attention mechanism remains a significant computational bottleneck, with quadratic time and memory complexity with respect to input sequence length. This limitation poses substantial challenges for scaling LLMs to handle increasingly long contexts with both strong performance and high efficiency. To address this, two major directions have emerged to reduce the time and space complexity of softmax Attention. The first mechanism is Linear Attention [17, 22, 50, 53, 70, 72], which seeks to reduce attention complexity by reparameterizing or approximating the softmax attention as linear operations. The second candidate is Sparse Attention [ 8, 21, 34, 56, 73], which restricts attention computation to a subset of the full key space based on fixed or dynamic sparsity pat- terns. While both approaches aim to improve efficiency, they differ significantly in formulation, design choices, and hardware implications. This survey provides a comprehensive review of recent developments in Efficient Attention mechanisms, with a dual focus on algorithmic principles and system-level implementation. Based on that, we also study the Pre-trained LLM employing these Efficient Attentions. We categorize linear attention methods into three major paradigms. First, kernelized linear attention approximates the softmax kernel with inner products in a feature space, achieving linear complexity via random feature maps [ 9, 42] or fixed positive mappings [ 22]. Second, recurrent linear attention with forgetting mechanisms introduces position-aware recurrence, enabling long-sequence modeling through data-independent [53] or data-dependent decay [17, 70], which control how past information fades over time. Third, fast-weight and meta-learning- based formulations reinterpret linear attention as a memory update process optimized online, where models such as DeltaNet [50, 72] and TTT [51, 52] incorporate fast-learning dynamics directly into the state evolution. We also examine hardware-friendly representations of linear attention-including parallel, recurrent, and chunkwise forms-highlighting their respective trade-offs in computational complexity, memory footprint, and compatibility with training or inference workflows. We classify Sparse Attention into fixed-pattern sparsity, block sparsity, and clustering-based sparsity. Fixed-pattern sparsity adopts static token-level masks such as sliding windows, dilated positions, or designated global tokens, offering simplicity and hardware-friendliness [4, 8, 14, 65]. Block sparsity selects or routes attention at block granularity, either via heuristic scoring [34, 56, 66], trainable gating [15, 73], enabling structured memory access and efficient GPU utilization. Clustering-based sparsity organizes key-value pairs using content-based or position-aware grouping methods such as k-means or Local Sensitive Hashing (LSH), facilitating semantically aware retrieval with reduced memory overhead [7, 24, 32]. Finally, we also discuss bidirectional sparse designs extend sparsity patterns to encoder-style models. These approaches differ in sparsity granularity, selection mechanism, and their alignment with hardware primitives like FlashAttention [10], and collectively represent the foundation for efficient long-context modeling in modern Transformers. There are recent efforts to integrate efficient attention mechanisms into industry-level Pre- trained Language Models. These include both pure efficient architectures-such as linear attention and state-space models, and hybrid designs that combine local and global attention patterns. Models like EAGLE [39], Falcon Mamba [79] and MiniCPM4 [58] demonstrate the scal- ability of purely linear or sparse approaches to the multi-billion parameter scale, offering strong performance with constant-time inference. Meanwhile, hybrid models [5, 26, 28, 33, 54, 57, 67] 3 interleave dense, sparse, and local attention to balance computational efficiency with context modeling capacity, reflecting a growing trend toward compositional, hardware-aware attention designs in modern LLMs. Our goal is to provide a unified framework for understanding the evolution of attention mechanisms under both algorithmic and hardware constraints, and how these designs are integrated into scalable LLM architectures. By connecting theoretical insights with practical im- plementations, we hope this survey offers a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners working toward efficient and deployable model design. This survey is motivated by a pivotal transition in the landscape of Large Language Models. While previous development was predominantly driven by a parameter-scaling paradigm aimed at maximizing capability, the current frontier has shifted toward an efficiency-centric orientation. As demands for million-token contexts and low inference cost, the quadratic time-space complexity of canonical self-attention constitutes the principal bottleneck inhibiting scalability. Consequently, the redesign of attention mechanisms has emerged as the critical frontier for architectural innovation. Synthesizing these developments is essential to bridge the disconnect between theoretical algorithmic design and the practical latencies imposed by modern hardware accelerators, thereby laying the groundwork for the next generation of scalable and commercially viable models. To structure this survey, we organize the discussion as follows: ? Section 2 introduces Linear Attention, covering its evolution across different model gener- ations, the associated design principles, and implications for hardware implementation. ? Section 3 presents Sparse Attention, categorizing sparsity patterns, analyzing deployment scenarios, and offering practical system-level design recommendations. ? Section 4 reviews Pre-trained Language Models that incorporate efficient attention mech- anisms, including both uniform efficient architectures and hybrid models that integrate local, sparse, and dense attention. ? Section 5 and 6 offers Takeaways and an Outlook on future directions, discussing open challenges and potential advances in algorithmic and hardware-aligned research. 2. Linear Attention 2.1. Linear Attention as In-Context Learners Beyond the efficiency gains offered by linear attention mechanisms, a significant advancement lies in their application to enhancein-context learning. This refers to the capability of a model to rapidly adapt or learn from a given prompt without requiring explicit gradient updates to its pre-trained weights. While large Transformer models inherently exhibit in-context learning by interpreting the prompt as a form of training data, recent innovations have integrated fast learning rules directly into the attention mechanism, effectively treating sequence processing as an online training process.FWP[ 50] establish a formal equivalence between existing linear attention mechanisms and fast weight learning. In the FWP paradigm, a slow neural network learns to program the "fast weights" of another network, often via additive outer products of self-invented key and value patterns. Bidirectional Linear Attention Bidirectional attention plays an important role in encoder-style architectures such as BERT [13]. The key difference in the linear formulation between unidirectional and bidirectional attention lies in the inference bottleneck and computational pattern. Encoder-only models typically exhibit?(? 2) complexity. Moreover, each token in an encoder-only model has access to global information. As a result, bidirectional linear attention often maintains a constant-length global token pool to reduce complexity while preserving the use of the softmax function. For instance, Linformer [63] reduces the number of keys and values to a constant length through an additional matrix projection. Luna [ 35] further extends the Linformer design by encoding the global token pool across model layers. Architecture of different stacked models. 4. Pretrained LLM with Efficient Attention 4.1. Pretrained Models with Uniform Efficient Attention While early explorations of linear attention were often confined to smaller-scale models, recent advancements have demonstrated their successful scalability to the multi-billion parameter range, establishing them as viable and highly efficient alternatives to the standard Transformer. These models, built purely on linear attention or its architectural equivalents like State-Space Models (SSMs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), retain their signature inference effi- ciency even at large scales. RWKV-based modelThe RWKV project represents a sustained and influential effort to create a scalable Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) architecture that combines the parallelizable training of Transformers with the efficient inference of traditional RNNs [38]. For instance, the EAGLE (RWKV-5) series introduced matrix-valued states to increase capacity, while subsequent iterations like Finch (RWKV-6) [39] and Goose (RWKV-7) [40] incorporated dynamic recurrence and expressive state evolution mechanisms (e.g., a delta-rule) to enable more complex, data- dependent state transitions. Mamba-based modelThe success of the Mamba architecture [ 17], with its data-dependent selection mechanism (Section 2.2.2), has spurred a wave of adoption and scaling initiatives from major research labs.Falcon Mamba[ 79] is based on the pure Mamba-based architecture to demonstrate performance competitive with leading Transformer models on a wide range of general-purpose language benchmarks, validating the architecture's viability for such tasks while retaining its signature constant-time inference. Further evidence of this paradigm's potential is provided byCodestral Mamba[ 36], built on the Mamba-2 architecture. While specialized for code generation, it achieves state-of-the-art results on relevant benchmarks and supports a 256k token context, demonstrating the scalability and effectiveness of the SSM approach within a complex and structured domain. Sparse-based modelMiniCPM-4 [ 58] introduces a two-stage sparse attention mechanism that dynamically selects relevant key-value blocks for each query token based on semantic similarity. MiniCPM-4 leverages InfLLM-v2, a Block Sparse Attention variant to replace standard 18 Attention mechanism. Moreover, a lightweight LogSumExp approximation enables efficient top- k selection, making the method scalable to extremely long sequences. Together, these techniques allow MiniCPM-4 to balance fine-grained contextual awareness with tractable memory and compute requirements, making it a strong candidate for long-context modeling. 4.2. Pretrained Models with Hybrid Efficient Attention With the increasing demand for efficient long-context modeling and diverse computational paradigms, recent research has extensively explored hybrid attention mechanisms. Such strate- gies combine global and local attention components, often interleaving specialized layers to balance computational cost and performance. The candidate model architecture illustrations are shown in Figure 4. Sparse Hybrid ModelGPT-3 [ 5] integrates a hybrid attention mechanism by interleaving dense and locally banded sparse attention layers, inspired by the Sparse Transformer [8]. Dense attention provides full-context modeling, while sparse layers adopt fixed or strided patterns to reduce the number of attended tokens. This design enables GPT-3 to efficiently scale to large model sizes using a fixed context window of 2048 tokens, balancing modeling capacity and computational efficiency. Linear-Full Hybrid ModelJamba [ 28] and MiniMax-01 [26] combine linear and full attention layers to achieve an efficient trade-off between throughput and expressiveness. MiniMax-01 employs Lightning Attention across most layers, inserting Softmax-based full attention every eight layers. Jamba adopts a similar ratio, inserting one Transformer layer into every eight-layer Mamba block. Both achieve faster decoding and improved long-sequence performance by limiting the use of computationally intensive full attention. Local-Full Hybrid ModelGemma 3 [ 57], Command A [ 67], and LLaMA-4-Maverick [ 33] alternate between local and global attention layers, with a shared design philosophy of using global layers sparsely, e.g., every 4-6 layers, to enhance efficiency. While local layers adopt sliding-window patterns, the key difference lies in position encoding strategies. Gemma 3 modulates RoPE base frequencies-assigning 10K for local and 1M for global layers-to better capture long-range dependencies. Command A and LLaMA-4-Maverick mixes RoPE-based local layers with full attention layers that omit positional embeddings entirely, allowing stronger long sequence performance. Advanced Hybrid ModelCharacter.AI [ 6] interleaves local attention with sliding windows and sparse global attention layers applied every six layers. Especially, they resue global attention layer's key-value representations across multiple non-adjacent layers. This KV sharing mecha- nism enables efficient long-context processing with reduced memory and latency overhead. YOCO [54] and Phi-4-mini-flash [48] adopt a dual-decoder architecture that separates the prefill and generation phases. The Self-Decoder utilizes linear attention mechanisms such as RetNet and Sliding-Window Attention for both prefill and generation, while the Cross-Decoder is activated only during generation. A single-layer global KV cache is used throughout, allowing linear-time prefill and efficient decoding with minimal GPU memory consumption. 19 In summary, these recent advances underscore the trend toward hybridizing attention mechanisms to achieve balanced performance across varying computational constraints and sequence lengths. Each architecture uniquely contributes insights into effectively combining local detail management with global context integration, thereby providing valuable frameworks for future attention mechanism developments. 5. TAKEAWAYS Based on the current trajectory of both academic research and industrial deployment, several key consensus points emerge regarding the design of efficient attention mechanisms. The Superiority of HybridityThere is a growing consensus that while purely linear attention architectures offer impressive inference speeds, they frequently incur a non-trivial performance penalty in complex reasoning and ultra-long context retrieval. Consequently, hybrid models have emerged as the preferred architecture. These designs not only maintain the near-lossless performance of standard Transformers but demonstrate the potential to exceed them by balanc- ing global associative memory with precise local retrieval. The OOM results for standard Transformer occur during training when maintaining consistent batch sizes across all sequence lengths for fair comparison. With standard data parallelism, each GPU maintains a complete copy of the model, optimizer states, and gradients; thus, the 840GB = 320GB total memory cannot be pooled, and each GPU independently faces the 40GB memory constraint. The quadratic memory footprint includes: (1) the attention matrices (approximately 32GB per layer for batch size of 16 at 8192 tokens with mixed precision), (2) activation storage for backpropagation, (3) optimizer states (Adam requires 2 parameter memory), and (4) gradient accumulation. While it is possible to train longer sequences with reduced batch size or gradient checkpointing, we maintain consistent training configurations across all models for fair efficiency comparison. CPA demonstrates excellent scalability, with memory usage and computation time scaling linearly with sequence length. For short sequences (512 tokens), the efficiency gains are moderate compared to standard Transformers. However, as sequence length increases, the benefits become increasingly pronounced. At 8,192 tokens, standard Transformers run out of memory (OOM) on our hardware, while CPA continues to function efficiently. At 32,768 tokens, CPA maintains the lowest memory usage and highest inference speed among all compared models who went Out-Of-Memory. Figure 6 visualizes the scaling of memory usage with respect to sequence length, clearly showing the quadratic scaling of standard Transformers versus the linear scaling of CPA and other efficient attention variants. Analysis of learned attention patterns To better understand how CPA allocates attention, we visualize the sparse attention weights for different layers and heads on the WMT14 En-De translation task. Figure 8 shows attention visualizations for representative heads in different layers. Fig. 8. Open in a new tab Visualization of learned attention patterns in CPA. Each colored bar represents a token receiving non-zero attention, with color intensity indicating attention weight magnitude. (a-c) show patterns from different layers and heads, demonstrating increasing specialization from early to deeper layers. (d) shows average attention by position across all heads in the final layer. We observe several interesting patterns: Specialization by head: Different attention heads focus on different aspects of the input. Some heads attend primarily to content words (nouns, verbs), while others focus on function words or syntactic markers. Layer-specific behavior: Early layers (Figure 8a) tend to have more distributed attention, while deeper layers (Figure 8c) become increasingly focused on specific tokens that are semantically important for the current context. Context-dependent sparsity: The number of tokens receiving non-zero attention varies significantly based on the input complexity. Simple sentences result in very sparse attention (5-10% of tokens), while complex sentences with ambiguous references or specialized terminology lead to less sparse patterns (20-30% of tokens). Positional biases: Despite not explicitly encoding positional relationships in the attention mechanism, certain heads develop positional biases (Figure 8d), focusing on tokens near the beginning or end of the sequence. These observations suggest that CPA learns meaningful attention allocation strategies that adapt to input complexity, supporting our hypothesis that explicit pairwise comparisons are often redundant. Discussion Key findings Our experimental results demonstrate that Contextual Priority Attention achieves performance competitive with standard self-attention while significantly reducing computational costs. This supports our hypothesis that explicit pairwise token interactions may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. The global-to-local attention paradigm of CPA offers several advantages: Efficiency: Linear scaling with sequence length enables processing of much longer sequences than standard Transformers can handle. Our results show CPA can efficiently process sequences up to 32K tokens, where standard Transformers run out of memory. Interpretability: The sparse attention patterns highlight which tokens are most contextually relevant, providing insights into model decision-making. As shown in our analysis of attention patterns, CPA learns meaningful token prioritization strategies. Adaptivity: The number of tokens attended to naturally adapts to input complexity, allocating computational resources where needed. This results in more efficient processing of simple inputs while maintaining capacity for complex ones. Effectiveness on long sequences: CPA performs particularly well on long document tasks, where capturing both local and global context is essential. This makes it well-suited for applications like document-level machine translation, long-form question answering, and document summarization. Figure 9 illustrates the performance-complexity trade-off for different attention mechanisms. CPA achieves an attractive balance, delivering near-standard-Transformer performance with linear computational complexity. Fig. 9. Open in a new tab Performance vs. computational complexity for different attention mechanisms on the WMT14 En-De translation task. The ideal models would be in the top-left corner (high performance, low complexity). CPA achieves a favorable trade-off, approaching the performance of standard Transformers while maintaining linear complexity. Limitations Despite its promising results, CPA has several limitations that present opportunities for future research: Global context quality: The performance of CPA depends critically on the quality of the Global Context Vector. For very complex or ambiguous inputs, a single context vector may not capture all relevant aspects of the sequence. This limitation becomes more pronounced as sequence length increases beyond the sizes tested in our experiments. Task-specific performance: While CPA performs well across most tasks, it shows slightly lower performance on certain language modeling benchmarks. This suggests that some tasks may benefit more from exhaustive pairwise comparisons. Training dynamics: We observed that CPA models sometimes require more careful initialization and training compared to standard Transformers, likely due to the increased importance of the global context representation. Learning meaningful global representations early in training is crucial for model convergence. Theoretical capacity: While we prove that CPA can theoretically approximate standard attention, this approximation may require higher model capacity in practice. Our experiments compensated for this by slightly increasing the hidden dimensions in the priority scoring MLP. Hardware utilization: The sparse attention patterns in CPA, while theoretically efficient, may not fully utilize modern GPU hardware designed for dense matrix operations. Custom CUDA kernels for sparse operations help mitigate this issue but introduce additional implementation complexity. Future directions Our work opens several promising directions for future research: Hierarchical CPA: Creating hierarchical representations of global context at different granularities could help capture both fine-grained and high-level patterns. This approach would involve computing multiple context vectors at different levels of abstraction, from local windows to global document-level representations. Adaptive sparsity: Dynamically adjusting the sparsity level based on input complexity could further improve efficiency without sacrificing performance. This could be implemented by learning a threshold function that determines the minimum attention weight required for a token to be considered relevant. Causal CPA for auto-regressive generation: Our current implementation applies CPA only in encoder architectures. Extending CPA to efficient causal decoding in decoder-only models (like GPT-style architectures) requires careful design to handle incremental GCV updates. One promising approach is to maintain a running GCV that can be updated in time per generated token: . This would enable linear-time auto-regressive generation while maintaining the benefits of global context-driven attention. Cross-modal applications: The global context approach may be particularly well-suited for cross-modal attention, where different modalities (text, image, audio) require different attention patterns. For example, in multimodal tasks, separate global context vectors could be computed for each modality, then used to guide cross-modal attention. Theoretical exploration: Further theoretical analysis of the expressivity-efficiency tradeoff in different attention mechanisms could guide the development of even more efficient variants. This includes a deeper understanding of what types of dependencies can be captured by global-context-based attention versus explicit pairwise attention. Pre-training and transfer learning: Investigating how CPA performs in large-scale pre-training scenarios and subsequent fine-tuning could reveal its potential for more efficient foundation models. The linear scaling properties of CPA make it particularly promising for very large models trained on extensive datasets. Hardware optimization: CPA's sparse attention patterns could enable specialized hardware implementations for even greater efficiency gains. Future research could explore hardware designs specifically optimized for global-context-based sparse attention mechanisms. Figure 10 illustrates these potential future directions, highlighting their relative complexity and potential impact. We believe the hierarchical CPA and adaptive sparsity approaches represent the most immediate opportunities for significant improvements. Fig. 10. Open in a new tab Potential future directions for extending Contextual Priority Attention. Each path represents a promising avenue for research, with estimated complexity and potential impact. Conclusion We presented Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), a novel attention mechanism that achieves theoretical complexity while empirically demonstrating linear scaling and maintaining competitive performance with standard Transformers. By reimagining attention as a global-context-driven priority system rather than exhaustive pairwise comparisons, CPA offers significant efficiency improvements, particularly for long sequences. Our experimental results across diverse tasks demonstrate that CPA achieves performance comparable to full attention while scaling more efficiently to long inputs. The emergent attention patterns reveal that CPA learns meaningful prioritization strategies that adapt to input complexity. On the Long Range Arena benchmark specifically designed to test long-range modeling capabilities, CPA outperforms other efficient attention variants by a significant margin. The success of CPA suggests that the quadratic computational complexity of standard self-attention may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. By focusing computational resources on the most contextually relevant tokens, CPA provides an efficient alternative that scales better to the increasingly long contexts required by modern NLP applications. The ability to process sequences of tens of thousands of tokens efficiently opens up new possibilities for applications such as document-level translation, long-form question answering, and full-document summarization.
